claim: Forming an if-then plan (when situation X arises, I will do Y) raises the rate at which a goal is acted on, with a medium-to-large effect across many studies.
effect: d = 0.65 across 94 independent tests (meta-analysis)
population: adults and students; health, academic, work and everyday goals

sources.cite: Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119.

caveats: Works when the goal itself is wanted; the specific cue does the work, not the resolve. Weaker for goals the person is ambivalent about.
app: One tap says when: after pickup, after her bedtime, at the next check-in. The cue counts show which cue holds.

claim: Monitoring progress toward a goal, especially when the progress is recorded or made public, increases the chance the goal is reached.
effect: d = 0.40 on goal attainment across 138 studies; larger when progress was recorded (d = 0.53)
population: adults; health, work and academic goals

sources.cite: Harkin et al. (2016). Does monitoring goal progress promote goal attainment? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence. Psychological Bulletin, 142(2), 198–229.

caveats: The effect is on behaviour; it says nothing about mood. Monitoring that becomes grading can backfire; counts, not verdicts.
app: The proof ladder, follow-through counts and the last-moved line are monitoring; they carry part of the effect on their own.

claim: A new daily behaviour takes weeks to months to feel automatic, and missing a single day does not measurably set the process back.
effect: median 66 days to plateau, range 18 to 254 days, in 96 volunteers
population: adults choosing one new eating, drinking or activity behaviour

sources.cite: Lally et al. (2010). How are habits formed: modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 40(6), 998–1009.

caveats: One study, self-reported automaticity, a small sample; the 66-day figure is a median, not a rule.
app: A missed day is a fact, never a streak lost. The same cue on the same days is what builds the habit.

claim: A large change in intention produces only a small-to-medium change in behaviour; wanting to is not the bottleneck.
effect: a medium-to-large change in intention (d = 0.66) led to a small-to-medium change in behaviour (d = 0.36) across 47 experiments
population: adults; health and everyday behaviours

sources.cite: Webb & Sheeran (2006). Does changing behavioral intentions engender behavior change? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence. Psychological Bulletin, 132(2), 249–268.

caveats: Experimental studies only; the gap is smaller for behaviours under the person's direct control.
app: The brief never asks for more resolve. It asks for a cue, a smaller step, or a different alternative.

claim: The idea that willpower is a tank that drains with use did not survive a large pre-registered replication; a hard morning does not use up the evening's self-control.
effect: d = 0.04 across 23 laboratories and 2,141 participants, against an original claim of d ≈ 0.6
population: adults in laboratory tasks

sources.cite: Hagger et al. (2016). A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4), 546–573.

caveats: Tiredness and low energy are real and read directly; what failed is the specific tank model of self-control.
app: A low energy reading is a reason to shrink the step, not to skip the evening. The record, not a theory, says what tired does.

claim: Responding to a lapse with self-compassion rather than self-criticism increases the motivation to improve and to try again.
effect: four experiments; self-compassion induction raised motivation to improve and time spent studying for a retest
population: undergraduates recalling or experiencing a failure

sources.cite: Breines & Chen (2012). Self-compassion increases self-improvement motivation. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 38(9), 1133–1143.

caveats: Student samples and short-term outcomes; the effect on long-run behaviour is not shown here.
app: After a step ends in No, the offer removes the obstacle and never shrinks the aim; the wording stays plain and unjudging.

claim: People are more likely to begin working toward a goal right after a temporal landmark such as a new week, month, or birthday.
effect: field data on gym visits, goal searches and commitment contracts rise after landmarks; laboratory follow-ups vary
population: adults; archival and field data

sources.cite: Dai, Milkman & Riis (2014). The fresh start effect: temporal landmarks motivate aspirational behavior. Management Science, 60(10), 2563–2582.

caveats: Starting rises; persistence after the landmark is not shown to rise with it.
app: A Monday or the first of the month is a good day to restart a stalled step; it is not a reason to wait for one.

claim: Pairing a wanted-but-avoided activity with a pleasure allowed only during it raises how often the activity is done.
effect: gym visits rose 29 to 51 percent while audiobooks were restricted to the gym; the effect faded when the restriction was lifted
population: university staff and students, one field experiment

sources.cite: Milkman, Minson & Volpp (2014). Holding the Hunger Games hostage at the gym: an evaluation of temptation bundling. Management Science, 60(2), 283–299.

caveats: One field study; the gain did not survive the end of the restriction.
app: A study sitting can be paired with the one thing allowed only then; the record can tell whether it held.

claim: What happens by default is done far more often than what needs a choice; setting the default is a stronger lever than deciding each time.
effect: d = 0.68 across 58 studies; larger for consumer and environmental domains, smaller for health
population: adults; policy, consumer and health choices

sources.cite: Jachimowicz et al. (2019). When and why defaults influence decisions: a meta-analysis of default effects. Behavioural Public Policy, 3(2), 159–186.

caveats: Most studies are one-shot choices, not daily habits.
app: The one offer per block and the pre-filled step are defaults on purpose: nothing to decide, one tap to accept or decline.

claim: Setting a specific goal changes behaviour more than a vague intention, with a small-to-medium effect.
effect: d = 0.34 on behaviour across 141 papers; larger when goals were set face to face or publicly
population: adults; health, work and academic behaviours

sources.cite: Epton, Currie & Armitage (2017). Unique effects of setting goals on behavior change: systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 85(12), 1182–1198.

caveats: Difficulty and specificity interact; a specific goal that is too hard can lower persistence.
app: A step is one line sized to one sitting, never a subject or a wish.

claim: Tangible rewards for an activity that was already interesting reduce later free-choice engagement in it.
effect: d = −0.34 on free-choice behaviour for expected tangible rewards across 128 studies; verbal praise did not undermine
population: children and adults in laboratory and field tasks

sources.cite: Deci, Koestner & Ryan (1999). A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation. Psychological Bulletin, 125(6), 627–668.

caveats: A long dispute over moderators; unexpected rewards and informational feedback do not show the effect.
app: No badges, no streaks, no points. Counts of what was done, and the reading the next morning.

claim: Periodic prompts and reminders help people keep to a health behaviour, especially when the prompt names the behaviour and arrives at a relevant time.
effect: systematic review of 19 studies: most found prompts effective; frequency and personal relevance mattered
population: adults in health promotion programmes

sources.cite: Fry & Neff (2009). Periodic prompts and reminders in health promotion and health behavior interventions: systematic review. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 11(2), e16.

caveats: Older studies, mixed quality; a prompt that arrives at the wrong moment is ignored.
app: A push at the cue time carrying the planned step, not a push at a fixed hour.

claim: People predict their own tasks will finish sooner than they do, even when they know their past tasks ran late.
effect: in the original studies fewer than half of students finished by their own predicted date
population: students and adults predicting task completion

sources.cite: Buehler, Griffin & Ross (1994). Exploring the planning fallacy: why people underestimate their task completion times. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 67(3), 366–381.

caveats: Effect sizes vary by task; using past records to predict reduces the bias.
app: A step is sized to one sitting because the sitting is what gets done; the record says how long things really take.

claim: Interventions that teach self-monitoring together with goal setting, feedback and review change physical activity and eating more than those without them.
effect: interventions with self-monitoring plus at least one other self-regulation technique were about twice as effective (d = 0.42 versus 0.26)
population: adults in physical activity and healthy eating trials, 122 studies

sources.cite: Michie et al. (2009). Effective techniques in healthy eating and physical activity interventions: a meta-regression. Health Psychology, 28(6), 690–701.

caveats: Technique coding across trials; individual differences are not separated out.
app: The check-in, the Done tap and the weekly view together are the self-monitoring the evidence points to.

claim: More options do not reliably reduce the chance of choosing; the average effect of choice overload across studies is near zero, and it appears only under particular conditions.
effect: mean effect near zero across 50 experiments, with real effects in some conditions such as no strong prior preference
population: adults in consumer and laboratory choice tasks

sources.cite: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd (2010). Can there ever be too many options? A meta-analytic review of choice overload. Journal of Consumer Research, 37(3), 409–425.

caveats: Moderators matter more than the headline; one move per block is a design choice, not a finding.
app: One offer per block is for the record's sake: one candidate per moment gives the learning a clean comparison.

claim: Practice spread over time is remembered better than the same practice massed into one session; the gap should grow with the delay until the material is needed.
effect: spaced practice beat massed in the large majority of 254 studies; the best gap scales with the retention interval
population: children and adults learning verbal material

sources.cite: Cepeda et al. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: a review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354–380.

caveats: Mostly verbal learning in the laboratory; the optimal gap depends on how long the memory must last.
app: Returning beats starting: the step follows the skill moved most recently, and short sittings on several days beat one long one.

claim: Retrieving something from memory strengthens it more than restudying it; practice tests beat rereading for later recall.
effect: g = 0.50 for testing over restudy across 159 effect sizes; g = 0.61 in a second meta-analysis of 118 studies
population: students and adults; classroom and laboratory

sources.cite: Rowland (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: a meta-analytic review of the testing effect. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1432–1463.
Adesope, Trevisan & Sundararajan (2017). Rethinking the use of tests: a meta-analysis of practice testing. Review of Educational Research, 87(3), 659–701.

caveats: Largest with feedback and with a delay before the final test.
app: The ladder's from-memory rungs are retrieval practice; explaining from memory is the proof, not another read-through.

claim: Mixing different kinds of problems or skills within a session improves later learning compared with practising one kind at a time, especially when the kinds are easily confused.
effect: g = 0.42 overall across 238 effect sizes; larger for similar categories, smaller or absent for very different ones
population: students and adults; mathematics, categories, motor and perceptual tasks

sources.cite: Brunmair & Richter (2019). Similarity matters: a meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin, 145(11), 1029–1052.

caveats: Feels harder while learning, which is why people avoid it; the gain shows on the later test.
app: Two skills under one subject alternated across sittings is fine; the ladder does not require finishing one first.

claim: Practice testing and distributed practice have high utility across learners and materials; rereading, highlighting and summarising have low utility.
effect: ten techniques reviewed; two rated high utility, three moderate, five low
population: students across ages and subjects

sources.cite: Dunlosky et al. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques: promising directions from cognitive and educational psychology. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58.

caveats: Utility ratings are the authors' synthesis; some low-utility techniques help as a first pass.
app: The first rung is watched or read once; every rung after it is doing, building, breaking or explaining.

claim: Teaching material to someone else, or preparing to, improves the teacher's own retention, largely because teaching forces retrieval.
effect: teaching without notes improved retention as much as retrieval practice did; teaching with notes did not
population: undergraduates learning a science passage

sources.cite: Koh, Lee & Lim (2018). The learning benefits of teaching: a retrieval practice hypothesis. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 32(3), 401–410.

caveats: One study; the benefit depends on teaching from memory rather than reading from notes.
app: Explained from memory is a rung because it is retrieval; reading notes aloud would not be.

claim: Deliberate practice explains a real but limited share of performance differences: more in games, music and sport, little in education and professions.
effect: practice explained 26% of variance in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education and under 1% in professions across 88 studies
population: learners and performers across domains

sources.cite: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald (2014). Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis. Psychological Science, 25(8), 1608–1618.

caveats: Disputed by the original practice researchers over what counts as deliberate; the share is large enough to matter for an instrument. A published correction exists (DOI 10.1177/0956797618769891); the figures above are as corrected.
app: For an instrument or a craft, sittings compound; for a certification, what is practised matters more than how long.

claim: Rehearsing a task in the mind, without moving, improves later performance, most for tasks with a cognitive component and less as time passes without physical practice.
effect: d = 0.53 overall across 35 studies; weaker than physical practice, stronger than none
population: adults learning motor and cognitive tasks

sources.cite: Driskell, Copper & Moran (1994). Does mental practice enhance performance? Journal of Applied Psychology, 79(4), 481–492.

caveats: Older meta-analysis; the gain decays over weeks unless refreshed.
app: A piece can be rehearsed in the head in a spare ten minutes; it counts as a sitting on the way to from memory.

claim: Spaced practice sessions produce better skill performance than the same practice massed, for physical as well as mental tasks.
effect: d = 0.46 favouring spaced practice across 63 studies; larger for simple tasks
population: adults learning motor and cognitive skills

sources.cite: Donovan & Radosevich (1999). A meta-analytic review of the distribution of practice effect: now you see it, now you don't. Journal of Applied Psychology, 84(5), 795–805.

caveats: The best spacing depends on task complexity; very complex tasks show smaller gains.
app: Ten minutes on the scale most evenings beats an hour on Saturday; the ladder is built for that.

claim: Sleep after learning strengthens what was learned, for facts and for motor skills alike.
effect: review of experimental and physiological studies; sleep-dependent gains in declarative and procedural memory
population: adults and animals in laboratory studies

sources.cite: Rasch & Born (2013). About sleep's role in memory. Physiological Reviews, 93(2), 681–766.

caveats: Effect sizes vary by task; sleep loss the night after learning costs more than sleep loss before it.
app: A study sitting after her bedtime is well placed: sleep follows it. A short night after it costs the sitting some of its value.

claim: Exercise a few hours after learning, not immediately after, improved memory for the material two days later.
effect: 72 participants; exercise four hours after learning improved retention and hippocampal pattern similarity; immediate exercise did not
population: healthy adults in one experiment

sources.cite: van Dongen et al. (2016). Physical exercise performed four hours after learning improves memory retention and increases hippocampal pattern similarity during retrieval. Current Biology, 26(13), 1722–1727.

caveats: One study, not yet replicated; the timing window is approximate.
app: A workout day and a study sitting on the same day are not in competition; the record can test the order.

claim: Spacing the retrieval of new second-language words across a session and across days improves their retention; the size of the gaps matters less than that there are gaps.
effect: spaced retrieval beat massed; expanding and equal spacing did not differ reliably
population: adult learners of English vocabulary

sources.cite: Nakata (2015). Effects of expanding and equal spacing on second language vocabulary learning: does gradually increasing spacing increase vocabulary learning? Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 37(4), 677–711.

caveats: One learner population and one language; the general spacing result is the stronger claim.
app: A word or a rule on the language ladder is met again on another day before it climbs to from memory.

claim: Conversation with another person, with its clarifications and corrections, produces measurably more second-language learning than exposure without interaction.
effect: meta-analyses of interaction studies: medium-to-large effects on immediate and delayed measures (d around 0.75 in one synthesis)
population: adult second-language learners in classroom and laboratory studies

sources.cite: Mackey & Goo (2007). Interaction research in SLA: a meta-analysis and research synthesis. In Mackey (Ed.), Conversational interaction in second language acquisition (pp. 407–452). Oxford University Press.
Plonsky & Gass (2011). Quantitative research methods, study quality, and outcomes: the case of interaction research. Language Learning, 61(2), 325–366.

caveats: A book chapter; effect sizes vary by outcome and by how interaction was arranged.
app: Used with someone is the top rung of the language ladder because exchange is where the learning is measured.

claim: Caffeine taken six hours before bed still shortens and disturbs sleep, even when the person does not notice it.
effect: 400 mg at 0, 3 or 6 hours before bed cut objective sleep by more than an hour; the 6-hour dose was not noticed subjectively
population: twelve healthy adults, double-blind crossover

sources.cite: Drake et al. (2013). Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, 9(11), 1195–1200.

caveats: A small sample and a large dose; sensitivity varies widely between people.
app: Caffeine is reported by band at each check-in; Evidence sets the next nights after the bands against each other, like for like.

claim: Caffeine's half-life in healthy adults is around five hours, and varies from under two to over nine with genetics, smoking, pregnancy and medication.
effect: pharmacology review; half-life commonly 2.5 to 4.5 hours in adults, longer in many
population: adults; pharmacological studies

sources.cite: Fredholm et al. (1999). Actions of caffeine in the brain with special reference to factors that contribute to its widespread use. Pharmacological Reviews, 51(1), 83–133.

caveats: A review without a single effect size; individual variation is the point.
app: Half of a midday coffee is still there at bedtime for many people; the record can show whether that is true here.

claim: Across trials, caffeine shortened the night’s sleep by about 45 minutes; about 107 mg stopped shortening it only when taken 8.8 hours or more before bed, and about 217 mg only at 13.2 hours or more.
effect: meta-analysis of 24 studies: total sleep 45 minutes shorter, sleep efficiency 7% lower, 9 more minutes to fall asleep, 12 more minutes awake after sleep onset, less deep sleep
population: adults in controlled studies of caffeine taken before night-time sleep

sources.cite: Gardiner et al. (2023). The effect of caffeine on subsequent sleep: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine Reviews, 69, 101764.

caveats: The cut-offs are modelled from pooled studies with different doses and timings, not tested directly, and sensitivity varies widely between people.
app: The late-caffeine line uses these cut-offs, and only a reported band of 100 mg or more can fire it; an untapped window never does, and no bedtime is assumed.

claim: In daily caffeine users, much of the lift from the day’s first caffeine may be the reversal of overnight withdrawal rather than a gain above baseline; how much is contested.
effect: after overnight abstinence, caffeine restored the alertness withdrawal had taken from regular users and gave non- or low users little but jitteriness; other trials found gains in non-consumers, and attention gains without withdrawal
population: habitual and non-habitual caffeine users in double-blind laboratory trials

sources.cite: James & Rogers (2005). Effects of caffeine on performance and mood: withdrawal reversal is the most plausible explanation. Psychopharmacology, 182(1), 1–8.
Rogers, Heatherley, Mullings & Smith (2013). Faster but not smarter: effects of caffeine and caffeine withdrawal on alertness and performance. Psychopharmacology, 226(2), 229–240.
Haskell, Kennedy, Wesnes & Scholey (2005). Cognitive and mood improvements of caffeine in habitual consumers and habitual non-consumers of caffeine. Psychopharmacology, 179(4), 813–825.
Addicott & Laurienti (2009). A comparison of the effects of caffeine following abstinence and normal caffeine use. Psychopharmacology, 207(3), 423–431.

caveats: Contested: the last two trials found gains in non-consumers and in users who were not withdrawn. Kept as a caveat, never as a verdict.
app: Beside any same-check-in caffeine comparison for someone who reports caffeine on most days: part of the difference may be withdrawal, not a lift.

claim: Caffeine’s anxiety rises with the dose: 50 mg did not raise it in light users, 150 mg did in those with a sensitive gene variant, and 450 mg did in most; regular users grow largely tolerant to it.
effect: 102 light users given 0, 50, 150 and 450 mg in separate double-blind sessions: anxiety at 150 mg tracked the ADORA2A variant and 450 mg raised it in most; in 379 more, the same variant carried more anxiety and medium or high users showed a smaller anxiety response
population: healthy adults: light users in the first trial; non- or low and medium or high users in the second

sources.cite: Childs et al. (2008). Association between ADORA2A and DRD2 polymorphisms and caffeine-induced anxiety. Neuropsychopharmacology, 33(12), 2791–2800.

Rogers et al. (2010). Association of the anxiogenic and alerting effects of caffeine with ADORA2A and ADORA1 polymorphisms and habitual level of caffeine consumption. Neuropsychopharmacology, 35(9), 1973–1983.

caveats: Laboratory capsules in single sittings; genotype is unknown here, so the band is the only handle on dose, and anxiety is read here through Stress and Irritation, not measured directly.
app: The bands’ cut points sit where these doses fall; Stress read beside a band of 200 mg or more is shown as an association only.

claim: Self-reported sleep can understate a caffeine cost that measured sleep shows, and in daily life the link can be absent even when measured, so a record showing no difference says little either way.
effect: 400 mg six hours before bed cut measured sleep by more than an hour, while the sleep diary’s 41-minute drop did not reach significance; across 5,164 nights of 785 adults, evening caffeine showed no link with sleep measured at home
population: twelve healthy adults in a home crossover trial; 785 adults, mean age 64, in their own homes

sources.cite: Drake, Roehrs, Shambroom & Roth (2013). Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, 9(11), 1195–1200.

Spadola et al. (2019). Evening intake of alcohol, caffeine, and nicotine: night-to-night associations with sleep duration and continuity among African Americans in the Jackson Heart Sleep Study. Sleep, 42(11), zsz136.

caveats: One small trial with a large dose and one observational cohort; neither used bands like these.
app: The fixed wording when caffeine and sleep show no difference: no difference is showing, and self-reported sleep is known to miss caffeine’s effect.

claim: A short daytime nap improves alertness and cognitive performance afterwards.
effect: meta-analysis of 11 studies: naps improved cognitive performance overall, with alertness and memory the clearest gains
population: healthy adults, mostly young

sources.cite: Dutheil et al. (2021). Effects of a short daytime nap on the cognitive performance: a systematic review and meta-analysis. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 18(19), 10212.

caveats: Mostly young adults; benefits depend on nap length and time of day.
app: Napped today is an evening chip; the mornings after say what a nap does to the night here.

claim: Grogginess after waking is worse after longer naps that reach deep sleep; naps under about thirty minutes limit it.
effect: review of countermeasures; inertia lasts minutes to an hour, worse from slow-wave sleep
population: adults in laboratory and shift-work studies

sources.cite: Hilditch, Dorrian & Banks (2016). Time to wake up: reactive countermeasures to sleep inertia. Industrial Health, 54(6), 528–541.

caveats: A narrative review; individual thresholds vary.
app: A long afternoon nap can cost the evening block and the night; the chip and the evening reading show it.

claim: Short sleep affects mood more than it affects thinking or physical performance.
effect: meta-analysis of 19 studies: mood was the most affected outcome, with effects larger than for cognitive and motor performance
population: adults under partial and total sleep deprivation

sources.cite: Pilcher & Huffcutt (1996). Effects of sleep deprivation on performance: a meta-analysis. Sleep, 19(4), 318–326.

caveats: Older laboratory studies; partial sleep loss over days matters most for everyday life.
app: A low morning reading after a short night is expected, not a verdict; the sleep readings sit beside the mood reading for this reason.

claim: Keeping sleep and wake times regular predicts health outcomes independently of sleep duration, and in one large cohort more strongly.
effect: in 60,977 adults, sleep regularity predicted all-cause mortality more strongly than duration did
population: UK Biobank adults with wearable data

sources.cite: Windred et al. (2024). Sleep regularity is a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration: a prospective cohort study. Sleep, 47(1), zsad253.

caveats: Observational; regularity may mark other health behaviours.
app: A bedtime kept on study nights and on rest nights alike is worth more than an early one now and then.

claim: A warm bath or shower one to two hours before bed shortens the time it takes to fall asleep.
effect: meta-analysis of 17 studies: sleep onset about ten minutes faster with water at 40 to 42.5 °C, 1 to 2 hours before bed
population: adults, mostly healthy

sources.cite: Haghayegh et al. (2019). Before-bedtime passive body heating by warm shower or bath to improve sleep: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine Reviews, 46, 124–135.

caveats: Small studies; timing matters, right before bed helps less.
app: The warm shower is a passive item: it rides alongside a move and is read like for like against the mornings after.

claim: Reading on a light-emitting screen before bed delays melatonin and sleep onset compared with a printed page, by a modest amount.
effect: twelve adults, crossover: sleep onset about ten minutes later, melatonin suppressed, less next-morning alertness
population: healthy young adults in a laboratory

sources.cite: Chang et al. (2015). Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 112(4), 1232–1237.

caveats: A bright screen at full brightness for hours; dimmer, shorter use shows smaller effects in later studies.
app: Screen-free half hour is a catalogue move; the record says whether the mornings after differ here.

claim: Regular exercise improves sleep quality and shortens sleep onset by a small-to-medium amount; a single session helps a little the same night.
effect: meta-analysis of 66 studies: regular exercise small-to-medium effects on total sleep time, onset and quality; acute exercise small effects
population: adults across ages and fitness

sources.cite: Kredlow et al. (2015). The effects of physical activity on sleep: a meta-analytic review. Journal of Behavioral Medicine, 38(3), 427–449.

caveats: Late intense exercise can delay sleep for some; the average effect is favourable.
app: A workout day, read from the other app, is set against the night and the next morning like for like.

claim: Writing tomorrow's to-do list for five minutes before bed shortened the time to fall asleep compared with writing about completed tasks.
effect: 57 adults in a sleep laboratory: about nine minutes faster sleep onset; more specific lists helped more
population: healthy young adults, one night each

sources.cite: Scullin et al. (2018). The effects of bedtime writing on difficulty falling asleep: a polysomnographic study comparing to-do lists and completed activity lists. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 147(1), 139–146.

caveats: One laboratory night; not yet replicated in the home.
app: Planning the next study step at the end of the evening is a catalogue move; it may also serve the night.

claim: Scheduling and doing small rewarding or necessary activities, regardless of mood, lifts low mood with a large effect in trials.
effect: d = 0.87 against control conditions across 16 studies of behavioural activation for depression
population: adults with depressive symptoms

sources.cite: Cuijpers, van Straten & Warmerdam (2007). Behavioral activation treatments of depression: a meta-analysis. Clinical Psychology Review, 27(3), 318–326.

caveats: Clinical samples; the mechanism, action before mood, is what transfers to a low stretch.
app: When a stretch is starting, one easy move a day, kept, is the intervention; the necessities chips watch the same thing.

claim: Exercise reduces depressive symptoms with a large effect, and the effect holds after correcting for publication bias.
effect: SMD = 1.11 in 25 trials of exercise for depression, after adjustment for publication bias
population: adults with depression

sources.cite: Schuch et al. (2016). Exercise as a treatment for depression: a meta-analysis adjusting for publication bias. Journal of Psychiatric Research, 77, 42–51.

caveats: Supervised, structured programmes in trials; the size of the everyday effect is smaller.
app: Workout days from the other app are set against the evenings like for like; movement moves are in the catalogue for the afternoon dip.

claim: A brief walk of around twelve minutes raises positive mood at once, even without expectation that it will.
effect: three experiments: walking raised positive affect versus sitting, indoors and out, regardless of expectations
population: undergraduates

sources.cite: Miller & Krizan (2016). Walking facilitates positive affect (even when expecting the opposite). Emotion, 16(5), 775–785.

caveats: Student samples and short follow-up; the lift is immediate and modest.
app: The ten-minute walk targets mood in the afternoon block; its card says whether the record agrees.

claim: A walk in a natural setting reduced rumination and its neural signature compared with a walk of the same length in an urban setting.
effect: 38 adults, 90-minute walk: self-reported rumination fell and subgenual prefrontal activity decreased after the nature walk only
population: healthy urban adults

sources.cite: Bratman et al. (2015). Nature experience reduces rumination and subgenual prefrontal cortex activation. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 112(28), 8567–8572.

caveats: One study, a long walk; the general nature effect on attention is better supported.
app: Outdoors is a learned tag on moves; the record estimates its effect on its own.

claim: Time in natural settings restores directed attention, with medium effects on working memory and attentional control.
effect: meta-analysis of 42 studies: working memory d ≈ 0.5, cognitive flexibility and attentional control small-to-medium
population: adults and children in experimental studies

sources.cite: Stevenson, Schilhab & Bentsen (2018). Attention Restoration Theory II: a systematic review to clarify attention processes affected by exposure to natural environments. Journal of Toxicology and Environmental Health, Part B, 21(4), 227–268.

caveats: Heterogeneous measures; many short exposures in the laboratory.
app: An outdoor move before a study sitting is a fair test to run as a card: focus that evening against the alternative.

claim: Breaks of a few minutes during work raise vigour and reduce fatigue; effects on task performance are small and depend on the task.
effect: meta-analysis of 22 studies: vigour d = 0.36, fatigue d = 0.35, performance small and task-dependent
population: adults in work and laboratory tasks

sources.cite: Albulescu et al. (2022). "Give me a break!" A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of micro-breaks for increasing well-being and performance. PLoS ONE, 17(8), e0272460.

caveats: Short follow-ups; longer breaks may be needed for creative tasks.
app: Nothing extra is a real offer; a short break is one of the smallest moves and one of the best supported for energy.

claim: Reinterpreting a situation changes the feeling it produces; reappraisal is among the most effective regulation strategies, and suppression among the least.
effect: meta-analysis of 306 effect sizes: reappraisal small-to-medium, distraction effective, suppression of expression small, suppression of the feeling ineffective
population: adults in laboratory emotion tasks

sources.cite: Webb, Miles & Sheeran (2012). Dealing with feeling: a meta-analysis of the effectiveness of strategies derived from the process model of emotion regulation. Psychological Bulletin, 138(4), 775–808.

caveats: Laboratory inductions; real-life intensity may reduce what reappraisal can do in the moment.
app: Cooling off after a clash is a chip; the steadying moves are reappraisal and distraction, never suppression.

claim: Putting a feeling into words reduces its intensity, without trying to change the feeling.
effect: review of experimental and neuroimaging studies: labelling reduces subjective and physiological arousal; effects modest
population: adults in laboratory studies

sources.cite: Torre & Lieberman (2018). Putting feelings into words: affect labeling as implicit emotion regulation. Emotion Review, 10(2), 116–124.

caveats: Modest effects; the mechanism is debated.
app: The check-in's five phrases per reading are labelling; answering honestly is itself a small regulation.

claim: Writing about feelings and stressful events has a small positive effect on health and wellbeing on average.
effect: r = 0.075 across 146 studies; larger with more sessions and private, unprompted writing
population: adults and students

sources.cite: Frattaroli (2006). Experimental disclosure and its moderators: a meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(6), 823–865.

caveats: Small on average; not everyone benefits and some feel worse briefly.
app: The one optional line on the evening check-in is enough; the record does not push journaling.

claim: Gratitude exercises have a small effect on symptoms of depression and anxiety, smaller than often claimed.
effect: g ≈ 0.29 against passive controls and smaller against active ones, across 27 studies
population: adults, mostly non-clinical

sources.cite: Cregg & Cheavens (2021). Gratitude interventions: effective self-help? A meta-analysis with implications for research and practice. Journal of Happiness Studies, 22, 413–445.

caveats: Short interventions and short follow-ups; the effect is real and small.
app: A gratitude move is offered like any other and judged by its card, not by its reputation.

claim: Doing something kind for another person raises the doer's wellbeing by a small-to-medium amount.
effect: d = 0.28 across 27 experimental studies
population: adults and children in experiments

sources.cite: Curry et al. (2018). Happy to help? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of performing acts of kindness on the well-being of the actor. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 76, 320–329.

caveats: Mostly immediate measures; long-run effects are less studied.
app: A kindness move belongs in the people family; connection is one of its learned tags.

claim: Slow, deliberate breathing exercises reduce self-reported stress by a small-to-medium amount compared with no intervention.
effect: g = −0.35 for stress across 12 randomised trials, similar for anxiety and depression
population: adults, clinical and non-clinical

sources.cite: Fincham et al. (2023). Effect of breathwork on stress and mental health: a meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials. Scientific Reports, 13, 432.

caveats: Heterogeneous protocols and risk of bias in many trials.
app: A one-minute breathing move is the smallest steadying move; it is offered when stress reads high.

claim: Mindfulness meditation programmes produce small-to-moderate reductions in anxiety, depression and pain after eight weeks.
effect: anxiety d = 0.38, depression d = 0.30, pain d = 0.33 at eight weeks, across 47 trials with 3,515 participants
population: adults with clinical and non-clinical conditions

sources.cite: Goyal et al. (2014). Meditation programs for psychological stress and well-being: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Internal Medicine, 174(3), 357–368.

caveats: No evidence that meditation beat active treatments such as exercise or medication.
app: Quiet prayer and stillness moves sit in the faith and steadying families and are judged by their cards.

claim: Listening to music reduces stress-related outcomes, both physiological and self-reported, with a medium effect.
effect: meta-analysis of 104 randomised trials: small-to-medium effects on physiological stress and medium on psychological stress
population: adults in medical and everyday settings

sources.cite: de Witte et al. (2020). Effects of music interventions on stress-related outcomes: a systematic review and two meta-analyses. Health Psychology Review, 14(2), 294–324.

caveats: Many trials in medical settings; effect on everyday stress may be smaller.
app: Music on purpose is a catalogue move and one of the alternatives a private item is compared against.

claim: Hunger makes negative feelings more likely in unpleasant situations, mostly when the person has not noticed the hunger.
effect: two online experiments and one laboratory study: hungry participants reported more negative emotion in negative contexts unless attending to their feelings
population: adults in the United States

sources.cite: MacCormack & Lindquist (2019). Feeling hangry? When hunger is conceptualized as emotion. Emotion, 19(2), 301–319.

caveats: Modest effects and one research group so far.
app: Hunger is a context reading beside mood; the necessities chips carry a missed meal.

claim: Mild dehydration worsens mood, fatigue and attention in healthy adults.
effect: review of experimental studies: consistent effects on mood and fatigue at 1 to 2 percent body-water loss; cognition mixed
population: healthy adults in laboratory studies

sources.cite: Masento et al. (2014). Effects of hydration status on cognitive performance and mood. British Journal of Nutrition, 111(10), 1841–1852.

caveats: Dehydration was often induced by exercise or heat, which confounds the mood effect.
app: A glass of water is among the smallest moves; it needs no more evidence than this to be offered.

claim: More time in daylight is associated with better mood and lower odds of depression, independently of exercise.
effect: in about 400,000 UK Biobank adults, each additional hour outdoors in daylight was associated with lower depression odds and better mood
population: middle-aged adults in the United Kingdom

sources.cite: Burns et al. (2021). Time spent in outdoor light is associated with mood, sleep, and circadian rhythm-related outcomes: a cross-sectional and longitudinal study in over 400,000 UK Biobank participants. Journal of Affective Disorders, 295, 347–352.

caveats: Observational and self-reported time outdoors.
app: Daylight is a rule on moves: the outdoor ones are offered inside your daylight hours, and outdoors is a learned tag.

claim: Stronger social relationships predict substantially longer survival, an association comparable to well-known health risks.
effect: 50 percent greater likelihood of survival for people with stronger relationships across 148 studies of 308,849 people
population: adults followed for an average of 7.5 years

sources.cite: Holt-Lunstad, Smith & Layton (2010). Social relationships and mortality risk: a meta-analytic review. PLoS Medicine, 7(7), e1000316.

caveats: Observational; causation runs both ways.
app: The loneliness reading is asked for this reason; conversations started is a count under your direction.

claim: Loneliness, social isolation and living alone are each associated with higher mortality, at similar sizes.
effect: 26 percent higher odds for loneliness, 29 percent for isolation, 32 percent for living alone across 70 studies
population: adults, mean age 66, followed for seven years on average

sources.cite: Holt-Lunstad et al. (2015). Loneliness and social isolation as risk factors for mortality: a meta-analytic review. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 10(2), 227–237.

caveats: Older samples on average; effects were similar for younger adults where measured.
app: Loneliness that reads high for a stretch is a warning the brief may raise, with a small contact as the move.

claim: Among ways of reducing loneliness, changing how a person reads social situations worked best; simply adding contact or support worked less.
effect: randomised trials addressing maladaptive social cognition had the largest effect (mean d ≈ −0.6); social-support and contact interventions smaller
population: adults and older adults in 50 studies

sources.cite: Masi et al. (2011). A meta-analysis of interventions to reduce loneliness. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 15(3), 219–266.

caveats: Few high-quality trials; the cognition finding rests on a handful of them.
app: Wanting more closeness while among people is a reading, not a contradiction; the reading's phrases were written for that.

claim: Days with more interactions with acquaintances, not only close ties, are days with more happiness and a stronger sense of belonging.
effect: two studies: within-person, more weak-tie interactions on a day predicted greater happiness and belonging that day
population: students and community adults

sources.cite: Sandstrom & Dunn (2014). Social interactions and well-being: the surprising power of weak ties. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 40(7), 910–922.

caveats: Correlational within days; direction not established.
app: One small contact, a message or a question to someone, is the people family's smallest move.

claim: People expect talking to a stranger to be unpleasant and find it more pleasant than expected; the mistaken expectation keeps them from doing it.
effect: commuters instructed to talk to a stranger reported a more positive experience than those told to keep to themselves, against their predictions; replicated across settings
population: commuters and adults in public settings

sources.cite: Epley & Schroeder (2014). Mistakenly seeking solitude. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(5), 1980–1999.
Schroeder, Lyons & Epley (2022). Hello, stranger? Pleasant conversations are preceded by concerns about starting one. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 151(5), 1141–1153.

caveats: Brief exchanges; the effect is on the moment, not on loneliness over months.
app: The people family's moves are small on purpose; the expected cost is the obstacle, not the exchange.

claim: People who ask more questions in conversation, especially follow-up questions, are liked more by their partners.
effect: in get-to-know-you conversations and speed dates, high question-askers were liked more; follow-up questions carried the effect
population: adults in live and online conversations

sources.cite: Huang et al. (2017). It doesn't hurt to ask: question-asking increases liking. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 113(3), 430–452.
Kluger & Malloy (2019). Question asking as a dyadic behavior. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 117(6), 1127–1138.

caveats: Contested and held as thin: a re-analysis found question asking as much a property of the pair as of the asker, and follow-up and switch questions largely the same (Kluger and Malloy 2019); one co-author has since had other papers retracted, not this one.
app: Ask one question is a move in the participation ladder; it is the smallest version of a conversation.

claim: Friendship takes time in the tens of hours: roughly fifty hours of shared time to move from acquaintance to casual friend, and two hundred to close friend.
effect: two studies of adults who had moved and of students: about 50 hours to casual friend, 90 to friend, 200 or more to close friend
population: adults and students forming new friendships

sources.cite: Hall (2019). How many hours does it take to make a friend? Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 36(4), 1278–1296.

caveats: Self-reported hours and retrospective estimates.
app: A conversation started is one count; the counts under your direction are how the hours accumulate.

claim: Behaving in an outgoing way lifts mood at the time and is followed by more fatigue some hours later.
effect: experience-sampling study: extraverted behaviour predicted higher positive affect at the time and greater fatigue three hours later
population: adults over twelve days of experience sampling

sources.cite: Leikas & Ilmarinen (2017). Happy now, tired later? Extraverted and conscientious behavior are related to immediate mood gains, but to later fatigue. Journal of Personality, 85(5), 603–615.

caveats: One study; the fatigue is modest and short-lived.
app: A big social event is an evening chip; the recovery gap is offered the day after, never as a verdict on the event.

claim: Regular attendance at religious services is associated with lower mortality, less depression and a greater sense of meaning in large cohorts.
effect: review of cohort studies: weekly attendance associated with about a quarter lower mortality and lower depression incidence
population: adults in the United States, mostly nurses and health professionals

sources.cite: VanderWeele (2017). Religious communities and human flourishing. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 26(5), 476–481.

caveats: Observational; the community, not belief alone, appears to carry much of the association.
app: Church day is a constant in the week's shape; faith is offered, never pushed, and its moves are judged by their cards.

claim: Volunteering is associated with lower depression and higher wellbeing in observational studies; trials are too few to say it causes them.
effect: systematic review of 40 studies: cohort studies show favourable associations; the five trials were inconclusive
population: adults and older adults

sources.cite: Jenkinson et al. (2013). Is volunteering a public health intervention? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the health and survival of volunteers. BMC Public Health, 13, 773.

caveats: Selection into volunteering is likely; the causal claim is not established.
app: Serving at church sits in the faith and people families; connection is its learned tag.

claim: A father's active engagement with a young child predicts fewer behaviour problems and better cognitive development later.
effect: systematic review of 24 longitudinal studies: engagement associated with better behavioural, social and cognitive outcomes
population: children followed from infancy and early childhood

sources.cite: Sarkadi et al. (2008). Fathers' involvement and children's developmental outcomes: a systematic review of longitudinal studies. Acta Paediatrica, 97(2), 153–158.

caveats: Observational and mostly two-parent households; engagement was measured many ways.
app: Time with her is a count under your direction and a family of moves; the count is the fact, never a grade.

claim: Reading with a young child is associated with stronger language and later reading skills, a relationship that holds across studies.
effect: meta-analysis of 99 studies: print exposure explained about 12 percent of variance in oral language in preschool, more later
population: children from preschool through university

sources.cite: Mol & Bus (2011). To read or not to read: a meta-analysis of print exposure from infancy to early adulthood. Psychological Bulletin, 137(2), 267–296.

caveats: Correlational; children who like language may seek more of it.
app: Reading with her is one of the moves in her family; her language skills on the checklist are the count beside it.

claim: A consistent bedtime routine for a young child is associated with earlier bedtimes, faster sleep onset and fewer night wakings, more so the more nights it is kept.
effect: 10,085 mothers in 14 countries: a dose-dependent association between routine nights per week and child sleep outcomes
population: children from infancy to five years

sources.cite: Mindell et al. (2015). Bedtime routines for young children: a dose-dependent association with sleep outcomes. Sleep, 38(5), 717–722.

caveats: Parent report, cross-sectional.
app: Her bedtime is the constant that ends the solo hours; a routine that holds is what makes the evening block usable.

claim: Praising a young child's effort and strategies, rather than the child, predicts a later belief that ability grows with work.
effect: parents' process praise at ages one to three predicted children's incremental beliefs at ages seven to eight in 53 families
population: children observed at home

sources.cite: Gunderson et al. (2013). Parent praise to 1- to 3-year-olds predicts children's motivational frameworks 5 years later. Child Development, 84(5), 1526–1541.

caveats: A small longitudinal sample; the wider mindset literature has had mixed replications.
app: Her checklist counts what she did and how much help she needed; the wording is about the doing.

claim: Parental burnout, distinct from job burnout and from depression, is linked to escape thoughts, neglect and violence toward children; recovery time for the parent is protective.
effect: two studies of about 2,000 parents: burnout predicted escape ideation, neglect and violence beyond depression and job burnout
population: parents in Belgium and the United Kingdom

sources.cite: Mikolajczak, Gross & Roskam (2019). Parental burnout: what is it, and why does it matter? Clinical Psychological Science, 7(6), 1319–1329.

caveats: Self-report and cross-sectional; the construct is newer than the others here.
app: The solo hours are a fact in the week's shape; the recovery gap and the steadying moves exist for the parent, not only the child.

claim: Switching between tasks carries a measurable cost in time and errors, even when the switch is predictable.
effect: review of task-switching experiments: reliable switch costs of hundreds of milliseconds that shrink with preparation but do not vanish
population: adults in laboratory tasks

sources.cite: Monsell (2003). Task switching. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 7(3), 134–140.

caveats: Laboratory tasks; the size of everyday costs depends on the tasks.
app: A study sitting is one skill, one rung; the focused block move is a single-task block.

claim: Interrupted work gets finished faster but at the price of more stress, frustration and effort.
effect: 48 participants: interruptions did not lengthen task time but raised stress, frustration, time pressure and effort
population: adults in a simulated office task

sources.cite: Mark, Gudith & Klocke (2008). The cost of interrupted work: more speed and stress. Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 107–110.

caveats: One laboratory study.
app: Quiet is a rule on some moves: they wait for a moment without her and without the office.

claim: People perform better at the time of day that matches their chronotype; morning types in the morning, evening types later.
effect: review of studies on attention, memory and executive tasks showing a synchrony effect, larger for demanding tasks
population: adults across chronotypes and ages

sources.cite: Schmidt et al. (2007). A time to think: circadian rhythms in human cognition. Cognitive Neuropsychology, 24(7), 755–789.

caveats: Effects depend on the task and on sleep the night before.
app: The usual reading per block is the record's own measure of this; the week ahead uses it.

claim: Alertness and performance dip in the early afternoon as part of the circadian rhythm, whether or not lunch was eaten.
effect: review: a reliable dip in alertness around 13:00 to 16:00, mostly circadian, larger after a short night
population: adults in laboratory and field studies

sources.cite: Monk (2005). The post-lunch dip in performance. Clinics in Sports Medicine, 24(2), e15–e23.

caveats: A narrative review; the size of the dip varies between people.
app: The afternoon block's usual reading often sits under the morning's; a short walk or a short nap are its moves.

claim: Making a concrete plan for an unfinished goal reduces the intrusive thoughts about it, even before anything is done.
effect: five experiments: writing a plan for an unfulfilled goal removed its interference with later tasks; merely thinking about it did not
population: undergraduates

sources.cite: Masicampo & Baumeister (2011). Consider it done! Plan making can eliminate the cognitive effects of unfulfilled goals. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 101(4), 667–683.

caveats: From a research programme with mixed replication history.
app: Write the exact next study step exists for this; one tap says when does the same for a step.

claim: If the next action takes under two minutes, doing it at once costs less than tracking it; a practitioner's rule with no trials behind it.
effect: a heuristic from a productivity method; no controlled evidence
population: none studied

sources.cite: Allen (2001). Getting Things Done: The Art of Stress-Free Productivity. Viking.

caveats: Thin evidence; kept because it is cheap and consistent with the small-step findings.
app: The two-minute rule is the unblock move for no time.

claim: Of the everyday events that lift mood and motivation at work, making progress on meaningful work, even small progress, was the most common.
effect: diary study of about 12,000 entries from 238 professionals; progress days were the best days
population: knowledge workers in seven companies

sources.cite: Amabile & Kramer (2011). The Progress Principle: Using Small Wins to Ignite Joy, Engagement, and Creativity at Work. Harvard Business Review Press.

caveats: A diary study reported in a book; correlational.
app: Partly counts as a start; the minimum win is one line sized to be met.

claim: People keep investing in a course of action because of what they have already put in, even when stopping would be better.
effect: a series of experiments: prior investment raised the willingness to continue a losing course
population: adults and students in decision scenarios

sources.cite: Arkes & Blumer (1985). The psychology of sunk cost. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 35(1), 124–140.

caveats: Scenario studies; the size in real decisions varies.
app: A card with many tries and no difference is retired or changed; the tries already made are not a reason to keep it.

claim: The finding that judges grew harsher before meal breaks, often cited as decision fatigue, is disputed: the order of cases can explain it.
effect: the original study reported favourable rulings falling toward each break; a re-analysis attributed the pattern to case scheduling
population: Israeli parole judges, archival data

sources.cite: Danziger, Levav & Avnaim-Pesso (2011). Extraneous factors in judicial decisions. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 108(17), 6889–6892.
Weinshall-Margel & Shapard (2011). Overlooked factors in the analysis of parole decisions. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 108(42), E833.

caveats: Kept as a disputed claim so the brief never cites decision fatigue as established.
app: Fewer decisions is a design choice for the record's sake; it is not backed by this.

claim: Ending a shower with cold water reduced sickness absence from work by about a third, without reducing the number of days people felt ill.
effect: randomised trial of 3,018 adults: 29 percent fewer sickness-absence days; no difference in illness days; many reported more energy
population: healthy adults in the Netherlands

sources.cite: Buijze et al. (2016). The effect of cold showering on health and work: a randomized controlled trial. PLoS ONE, 11(9), e0161749.

caveats: Unblinded, self-reported outcomes. A published correction exists (DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0201978).
app: A cold finish is a morning move for energy; its card will say what the afternoons after read.

claim: Short bouts of activity in green settings improve self-esteem and mood, with the largest gains in the first five minutes.
effect: multi-study analysis of 1,252 participants: self-esteem d = 0.46 and mood d = 0.54, largest for light activity and five-minute doses
population: adults in the United Kingdom

sources.cite: Barton & Pretty (2010). What is the best dose of nature and green exercise for improving mental health? A multi-study analysis. Environmental Science & Technology, 44(10), 3947–3955.

caveats: Pooled from the same group's studies; short-term measures.
app: Step outside for five minutes is a real move; the daylight rule keeps it inside the hours it can be done.

claim: More screen time at two and three years predicted slightly lower developmental screening scores a year later.
effect: 2,441 children: higher screen time at 24 and 36 months predicted lower scores at 36 and 60 months; small effects, one direction only
population: Canadian children followed from two to five years

sources.cite: Madigan et al. (2019). Association between screen time and children's performance on a developmental screening test. JAMA Pediatrics, 173(3), 244–250.

caveats: Parent-reported screen time; small effects; content and co-viewing not separated.
app: Her checklist and the moments with her are the counts; screens are not a chip and are not judged here.

claim: For social anxiety, individual cognitive-behavioural therapy had the largest effect of the psychological treatments; exposure with social-skills training, and self-help with support, also did better than waiting.
effect: network meta-analysis of 101 trials, 13,164 people: against a waiting list, individual CBT SMD −1.19, exposure and social skills −0.86, supported self-help −0.86; individual CBT was the psychological class to beat a psychological placebo
population: adults with social anxiety disorder in randomised trials

sources.cite: Mayo-Wilson et al. (2014). Psychological and pharmacological interventions for social anxiety disorder in adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. The Lancet Psychiatry, 1(5), 368–376.

caveats: Clinical samples; a curriculum of daily reps is not a treatment, and nothing here diagnoses anyone.
app: The Social path borrows its structure from what works for social fear: graded practice with real people, supported, never observed from a distance.

claim: Practice that varies reps, people and settings is recommended to make gains last, and does no harm, but its advantage over one fixed order is supported only in part.
effect: how far fear falls during practice did not predict outcome (Craske 2008); a meta-analysis found fear reduction within a session unrelated to outcome (Rupp 2017); a random or variable order did as well as a graded hierarchy in two small analogue trials; in a randomised trial the inhibitory-learning approach did no better on the primary outcome, with steeper self-reported gains on secondary ones (Treanor 2025)
population: anxious adults and analogue samples in exposure studies

sources.cite: Craske et al. (2008). Optimizing inhibitory learning during exposure therapy. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 46(1), 5–27.
Craske et al. (2014). Maximizing exposure therapy: an inhibitory learning approach. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 58, 10–23.

Rupp et al. (2017). Emotional processing theory put to test: a meta-analysis on the association between process and outcome measures in exposure therapy. Clinical Psychology & Psychotherapy, 24(3), 697–711.

Kircanski et al. (2012). Challenges to the traditional exposure paradigm: variability in exposure therapy for contamination fears. Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry, 43(2), 745–751.

Knowles et al. (2023). Facing uncertainty: a comparison of hierarchical and variable exposure interventions for contamination-related concerns. Journal of Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders, 36, 100777.
Treanor et al. (2025). A randomized controlled trial comparing two processes of exposure therapy: extinction learning and habituation. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology.

caveats: Mostly contamination and spider fears in small samples; the case for variety is a mechanism with mixed trials, which is why the path treats it as design judgment.
app: A stage holds several reps across kinds of setting, and no stage waits for you to feel calm.

claim: Dropping the small habits used to feel safe in conversation, and turning attention outward, made people come across better and feel better in experiments on social anxiety.
effect: people told to drop their own safety behaviours in a second conversation drew more positive reactions from the partner than graduated exposure alone (Taylor and Alden 2011); a cross-disorder meta-analysis of safety behaviours in exposure was inconclusive (Meulders 2016: SMD 0.31, not significant)
population: socially anxious adults in laboratory conversations

sources.cite: McManus, Sacadura & Clark (2008). Why social anxiety persists: an experimental investigation of the role of safety behaviours as a maintaining factor. Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry, 39(2), 147–161.

Taylor & Alden (2011). To see ourselves as others see us: an experimental integration of the intra and interpersonal consequences of self-protection in social anxiety disorder. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 120(1), 129–141.
Meulders et al. (2016). The use of safety-seeking behavior in exposure-based treatments for fear and anxiety: benefit or burden? A meta-analytic review. Clinical Psychology Review, 45, 144–156.

caveats: Single conversations in the laboratory; the meta-analysis across fears did not settle the question.
app: Every Social rep names an outward cue and the crutch to drop; a rep done with the crutch is honestly Partly.

claim: A week of short conversations with strangers made people less pessimistic about rejection and surer of their conversational ability, and the change lasted at least a week.
effect: a week-long scavenger hunt of approaching and talking to strangers, against controls: expectations grew more positive and accurate day by day, and the benefit held at least a week after
population: adults in a randomised field intervention

sources.cite: Sandstrom, Boothby & Cooney (2022). Talking to strangers: a week-long intervention reduces psychological barriers to social connection. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 102, 104356.

caveats: One study; the conversations were with strangers, and the effect on friendships is not measured.
app: The dose of the Social path: one rep a day at most, spread over days, never a streak.

claim: People expect a conversation with a stranger to go worse than it does, and those fears go with avoiding it.
effect: a mini meta-analysis across studies: predicted fears about starting, sustaining and ending conversations were larger than experience, and related to how much people talked
population: adults in several experiments and field studies

sources.cite: Sandstrom & Boothby (2021). Why do people avoid talking to strangers? A mini meta-analysis of predicted fears and actual experiences talking to a stranger. Self and Identity, 20(1), 47–71.

caveats: Conversations with strangers; how it generalises to people you know is less studied.
app: The Social path counts reps done, never how they went, because the going is usually better than the fear.

claim: Exposure spread over days held better at follow-up than the same exposure packed into one day, though packing sessions into weeks rather than months worked as well.
effect: expanding-spaced exposure over a week showed no return of fear at one month where massed exposure in a day did (Rowe and Craske 1998, n = 31); a multicentre trial found two-week intensified exposure equivalent to standard weekly exposure (Pittig 2021)
population: spider-fearful volunteers; adults with anxiety disorders in a multicentre trial

sources.cite: Rowe & Craske (1998). Effects of an expanding-spaced vs massed exposure schedule on fear reduction and return of fear. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 36(7–8), 701–717.
Tsao & Craske (2000). Timing of treatment and return of fear: effects of massed, uniform-, and expanding-spaced exposure schedules. Behavior Therapy, 31(3), 479–497.
Pittig et al. (2021). Efficacy of temporally intensified exposure for anxiety disorders: a multicenter randomized clinical trial. Depression and Anxiety, 38(11), 1169–1181.

caveats: Small early trials; the multicentre trial compared weeks with months, not days with hours.
app: One people rep a day across the whole app: spread, not packed.

claim: Disclosure and liking run both ways: people who share more are liked more, people share more with those they like, and taking turns in a first meeting builds closeness.
effect: a meta-analysis found all three disclosure-liking links (Collins and Miller 1994); structured, escalating turn-taking produced more closeness than small talk (Aron 1997); feeling responded to carried disclosure into intimacy in daily diaries (Laurenceau 1998); reciprocal turns raised liking in first meetings (Sprecher 2013)
population: adults and students in experiments, diaries and a meta-analysis

sources.cite: Collins & Miller (1994). Self-disclosure and liking: a meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin, 116(3), 457–475.
Aron et al. (1997). The experimental generation of interpersonal closeness: a procedure and some preliminary findings. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 23(4), 363–377.

Laurenceau, Barrett & Pietromonaco (1998). Intimacy as an interpersonal process: the importance of self-disclosure, partner disclosure, and perceived partner responsiveness in interpersonal exchanges. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(5), 1238–1251.
Sprecher, Treger & Wondra (2013). Taking turns: reciprocal self-disclosure promotes liking in initial interactions. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 49(5), 860–866.

caveats: Matching weight matters: a disclosure far heavier than the other person’s is not what was studied.
app: The matched-disclosure rep: answer something real with something of about the same weight, turn for turn.

claim: After a conversation, people underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
effect: across studies from first meetings in the laboratory to real acquaintances, partners liked people more than those people believed
population: students and adults in several studies

sources.cite: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018). The liking gap in conversations: do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science, 29(11), 1742–1756.

caveats: An average; any one conversation can go either way, which is why the path never asks how one went.
app: Behind the liking-gap note: one honest line about how it went, then the reminder beneath it.

claim: Deeper conversations with strangers felt less awkward and more connecting than people expected, because they expected others to care less about what they shared.
effect: over a dozen experiments: people overestimated awkwardness, most for deep talk, and felt more connected to deep than shallow partners after having both
population: adults and students in laboratory and online conversations

sources.cite: Kardas, Kumar & Epley (2022). Overly shallow? Miscalibrated expectations create a barrier to deeper conversation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 122(3), 367–398.

caveats: Structured prompts with strangers; depth pressed on an unwilling person was not studied.
app: The go-one-level-deeper rep at the Social path’s last stage.

claim: Listeners enjoyed hearing stories about experiences they had shared more than novel ones, though both speakers and listeners predicted the opposite.
effect: in two studies listeners enjoyed familiar stories much more than novel ones, not because of content or delivery
population: students in laboratory storytelling studies

sources.cite: Cooney, Gilbert & Wilson (2017). The novelty penalty: why do people like talking about new experiences but hearing about old ones? Psychological Science, 28(3), 380–394.

caveats: Laboratory stories; one paper.
app: The cue on the short-story rep: tell something the group has lived too.

claim: Acting more extraverted for a while raises positive feeling, introverts included, though introverts gain less and feel more tired and less authentic.
effect: people were happier in moments they acted extraverted (Fleeson 2002); a week of acting extraverted raised well-being (Margolis and Lyubomirsky 2020); in a randomised trial the benefit was weaker for introverts, with more negative feeling and tiredness and less authenticity (Jacques-Hamilton 2019)
population: students and adults in experience sampling and randomised trials

sources.cite: Fleeson, Malanos & Achille (2002). An intraindividual process approach to the relationship between extraversion and positive affect: is acting extraverted as “good” as being extraverted? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 83(6), 1409–1422.
Margolis & Lyubomirsky (2020). Experimental manipulation of extraverted and introverted behavior and its effects on well-being. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 149(4), 719–731.
Jacques-Hamilton, Sun & Smillie (2019). Costs and benefits of acting extraverted: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 148(9), 1538–1556.

caveats: Short manipulations; the cost for introverts is the reason reps are small and time-boxed.
app: Reps are small and specific and placed early in the day; the recovery gap follows a group rep (see the existing card on the cost three hours later).

claim: Practising social skills changes behaviour where watching others does not: skills training added to exposure beat exposure alone, and training effects on behaviour held where knowledge faded.
effect: social skills training with exposure gave better social skill and clinical status than exposure alone in a trial of 106 adults (Beidel 2014); a meta-analysis of behaviour modelling training found knowledge decayed while skills and behaviour held or grew (Taylor 2005)
population: adults with social anxiety; trainees in organisations

sources.cite: Beidel et al. (2014). The impact of social skills training for social anxiety disorder: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Anxiety Disorders, 28(8), 908–918.
Taylor, Russ-Eft & Chan (2005). A meta-analytic review of behavior modeling training. Journal of Applied Psychology, 90(4), 692–709.

caveats: No direct evidence that recording yourself or reading aloud transfers to conversation.
app: Solo rehearsal is a warm-up on the path and never moves a stage.

claim: Repeated contact in the same place builds ties: chance seating predicted friendship a year later, and the more strangers interacted, the more they liked each other.
effect: random seat assignment at a first class predicted friendship a year on (Back 2008); in live interaction, attraction rose with the amount of interaction, carried by responsiveness, comfort and knowledge (Reis 2011); a meta-analysis of repeated exposure found liking rises and then flattens (Montoya 2017)
population: students in field and laboratory studies; a meta-analysis of 268 curves

sources.cite: Back, Schmukle & Egloff (2008). Becoming friends by chance. Psychological Science, 19(5), 439–440.
Reis, Maniaci, Caprariello, Eastwick & Finkel (2011). Familiarity does indeed promote attraction in live interaction. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 101(3), 557–570.

Montoya, Horton, Vevea, Citkowicz & Lauber (2017). A re-examination of the mere exposure effect: the influence of repeated exposure on recognition, familiarity, and liking. Psychological Bulletin, 143(5), 459–498.

caveats: The exposure meta-analysis is mostly of images and sounds; the live-interaction work is short meetings.
app: Recurring places the week already holds are the home of both paths; errands add variety only.

claim: Specific charismatic tactics can be taught: trained speakers were rated more charismatic, though the studies are of speeches, not conversation, and small.
effect: training raised ratings of charisma, mean d = .62, in a field study of managers and a laboratory study of 41 MBA students (Antonakis 2011); everyday charisma splits into influence and affability, measurable and observable (Tskhay 2018)
population: managers and MBA students; adults in scale validation

sources.cite: Antonakis, Fenley & Liechti (2011). Can charisma be taught? Tests of two interventions. Academy of Management Learning & Education, 10(3), 374–396.
Tskhay, Zhu, Zou & Rule (2018). Charisma in everyday life: conceptualization and validation of the General Charisma Inventory. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 114(1), 131–152.

caveats: Speeches and small samples; held as modest.
app: Story, contrast and an animated voice belong to the group stage, marked as modest evidence.

claim: Randomising between acceptable options at each decision point gives honest short-term estimates of what helps, and the probabilities should be kept away from zero and one and logged.
effect: micro-randomised trials estimate proximal effects and how they change over time (Klasnja 2015); in one, a suggestion raised the next half hour of steps by 14 percent on average and the effect faded (Klasnja 2019); adaptive designs clip and record their probabilities (Liao 2020)
population: adults in mobile health studies

sources.cite: Nahum-Shani et al. (2018). Just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs) in mobile health: key components and design principles for ongoing health behavior support. Annals of Behavioral Medicine, 52(6), 446–462.
Klasnja et al. (2015). Microrandomized trials: an experimental design for developing just-in-time adaptive interventions. Health Psychology, 34(Suppl), 1220–1228.
Klasnja et al. (2019). Efficacy of contextually tailored suggestions for physical activity: a micro-randomized optimization trial of HeartSteps. Annals of Behavioral Medicine, 53(6), 573–582.

Liao, Greenewald, Klasnja & Murphy (2020). Personalized HeartSteps: a reinforcement learning algorithm for optimizing physical activity. Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies, 4(1), 18.

caveats: A design, not a finding about social skill; one person’s record is a small sample.
app: Where two or more reps fit the day, the app draws between them with logged, bounded probabilities, and only drawn offers enter comparisons.

claim: The claim that expansive “power poses” change hormones and confident behaviour is disputed: the hormone effects did not replicate, and what remains is small and comes from not slumping.
effect: a large replication found no effect on hormones or risk-taking (Ranehill 2015); a meta-analysis found effects driven by avoiding contractive postures (g = 0.45) rather than adopting expansive ones (g = 0.06) (Elkjær 2020); another meta-analysis of body positions reached a similar reading (Körner 2022)
population: adults in laboratory posture experiments

sources.cite: Ranehill et al. (2015). Assessing the robustness of power posing: no effect on hormones and risk tolerance in a large sample of men and women. Psychological Science, 26(5), 653–656.

Elkjær et al. (2020). Expansive and contractive postures and movement: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of motor displays on affective and behavioral responses. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 17(1), 276–304.

Körner, Röseler & Schütz (2022). Dominance and prestige: meta-analytic review of experimentally induced body position effects on behavioral, self-report, and physiological dependent variables. Psychological Bulletin, 148(1–2), 67–85.

caveats: Kept as disputed so the brain never cites power posing as established.
app: Excluded from the Social path.

claim: The advice to repeat positive self-statements is disputed: in two experiments people with low self-esteem who repeated one felt worse, and the finding stands unreplicated.
effect: repeating “I’m a lovable person” left low-self-esteem participants feeling worse, and helped high-self-esteem participants only a little
population: students in two experiments

sources.cite: Wood, Perunovic & Lee (2009). Positive self-statements: power for some, peril for others. Psychological Science, 20(7), 860–866.

caveats: Kept as disputed so affirmations are never offered as a rep.
app: Excluded from the Social path.

claim: Meeting online has become the most common way heterosexual couples in the United States meet, and people in thin markets, such as middle-aged heterosexuals, are especially likely to meet partners online.
