effect: a nationally representative 2017 survey: online meeting eclipsed meeting through friends around 2013 (Rosenfeld 2019); Internet access at home went with higher chances of having a partner, net of other factors (Rosenfeld and Thomas 2012)
population: nationally representative samples of US adults

sources.cite: Rosenfeld, Thomas & Hausen (2019). Disintermediating your friends: how online dating in the United States displaces other ways of meeting. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 116(36), 17753–17758.
Rosenfeld & Thomas (2012). Searching for a mate: the rise of the Internet as a social intermediary. American Sociological Review, 77(4), 523–547.

caveats: How couples meet describes the market, not what makes a relationship good.
app: Why the Partner path has an online channel at all: optional, bounded, off until chosen, and never a route to a stage.

claim: What online dating adds is access to people you would not otherwise meet; browsing many profiles side by side can turn people into a menu, and brief messaging that leads to meeting serves better than long browsing.
effect: a review of online dating’s three services, access, communication and matching: access is the clear benefit; the others are qualified
population: a review of research on online dating

sources.cite: Finkel, Eastwick, Karney, Reis & Sprecher (2012). Online dating: a critical analysis from the perspective of psychological science. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 13(1), 3–66.

caveats: A review from before most of today’s apps; read from the authors’ summary.
app: The online channel is short and points at meeting: one honest profile, a time-boxed browse, one message at a time, a short public meeting proposed soon.

claim: Online daters rated a first face-to-face meeting best after a moderate amount of messaging, and worse after very little or a great deal.
effect: a national sample of online daters: the relation between the amount of online contact before meeting and how the meeting went was curvilinear
population: a national sample of US online daters

sources.cite: Ramirez, Sumner, Fleuriet & Cole (2015). When online dating partners meet offline: the effect of modality switching on relational communication between online daters. Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication, 20(1), 99–114.

caveats: Self-report of a first meeting; the turning point is the authors’ estimate.
app: The online channel proposes a short public meeting within a few weeks of first contact, not after months of messages.

claim: The longer people browse dating profiles in a session, the more likely they are to reject each next one.
effect: across three studies, acceptance fell by about 27 percent from the first profile to the last in a session
population: adults viewing hypothetical and real dating profiles

sources.cite: Pronk & Denissen (2020). A rejection mind-set: choice overload in online dating. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 11(3), 388–396.

caveats: Session-level choices; what it means for relationships formed is not measured.
app: A browse is fifteen minutes and stops, whatever was found.

claim: About two-thirds of romantic relationships began as friendships, and the longer two people knew each other first, the less their pairing tracked consensus attractiveness and the more it rested on how they got on.
effect: a meta-analysis of seven samples (N = 1,897): two-thirds reported friends-first initiation (Stinson 2022); couples who knew each other longer before dating matched less on attractiveness (Hunt 2015); romantic evaluations were more unique to the pair than shared across raters (Eastwick and Hunt 2014)
population: students and crowdsourced adults; couples

sources.cite: Stinson, Cameron & Hoplock (2022). The friends-to-lovers pathway to romance: prevalent, preferred, and overlooked by science. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 13(2), 562–571.
Hunt, Eastwick & Finkel (2015). Leveling the playing field: longer acquaintance predicts reduced assortative mating on attractiveness. Psychological Science, 26(7), 1046–1053.
Eastwick & Hunt (2014). Relational mate value: consensus and uniqueness in romantic evaluations. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 106(5), 728–751.

caveats: Mostly students; relationships that begin as friendships may differ in other ways too.
app: The Partner path’s first stages share the Social path’s reps: the people your week already holds are where most of it starts.

claim: The traits people say they want in an ideal partner barely predict whom they come to desire in person, and more than a hundred measured traits could not predict which particular pairs would click.
effect: stated ideals failed to predict desire at a speed-dating event (Eastwick and Finkel 2008); machine learning on 100+ measures predicted none of the desire unique to a pair (Joel 2017); a worldwide registered report (N = 10,358) found matching on specific traits very small, average β = .04 (Eastwick 2025)
population: speed daters; adults in 43 countries

sources.cite: Eastwick & Finkel (2008). Sex differences in mate preferences revisited: do people know what they initially desire in a romantic partner? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 94(2), 245–264.
Joel, Eastwick & Finkel (2017). Is romantic desire predictable? Machine learning applied to initial romantic attraction. Psychological Science, 28(10), 1478–1489.
Eastwick, Luchies, Finkel & Hunt (2014). The predictive validity of ideal partner preferences: a review and meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 140(3), 623–665.
Eastwick et al. (2025). A worldwide test of the predictive validity of ideal partner preference matching. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 128(1), 123–146.

caveats: Physical attractiveness does predict initial evaluations moderately; ideals are not useless, only weak on specific traits.
app: No type list and no compatibility score anywhere in the path.

claim: Plain openings do best: a direct self-introduction or an introduction by a third person was rated most appropriate, and cute or flippant lines were rated worst.
effect: women and men rated cute-flippant opening lines least favourably (Kleinke 1986); among 642 students, third-party and direct introductions were rated most appropriate and the third-party one most effective (Weber 2010)
population: students rating opening lines

sources.cite: Kleinke, Meeker & Staneski (1986). Preference for opening lines: comparing ratings by men and women. Sex Roles, 15(11–12), 585–600.
Weber, Goodboy & Cayanus (2010). Flirting competence: an experimental study on appropriate and effective opening lines. Communication Research Reports, 27(2), 184–191.

caveats: Old, small, rated not lived; enough to rule lines out, not to write any.
app: The asking-a-friend and introduce-yourself reps; no lines anywhere in the path.

claim: People detect flirting poorly, and those who fear rejection believe their own overtures show far more interest than they do.
effect: observers were more accurate about conversations without flirting than with it (Hall 2015); four studies found a signal amplification bias in people afraid of rejection (Vorauer 2003)
population: students in laboratory and video studies

sources.cite: Hall, Xing, Ross & Silverman (2015). Accurately detecting flirting: error management theory, the traditional sexual script, and flirting base rate. Communication Research, 42(7), 939–958.
Vorauer, Cameron, Holmes & Pearce (2003). Invisible overtures: fears of rejection and the signal amplification bias. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 84(4), 793–812.

caveats: Laboratory judgements of strangers.
app: No rep reads signals; the say-your-interest-plainly rep says it in one sentence instead.

claim: People are less willing to turn down someone who asks them out in person than they predict, largely out of concern for the asker’s feelings.
effect: participants who believed the situation was real rejected unsuitable dates less than those imagining it, partly explained by not wanting to hurt the asker
population: single adults in laboratory studies

sources.cite: Joel, Teper & MacDonald (2014). People overestimate their willingness to reject potential romantic partners by overlooking their concern for other people. Psychological Science, 25(12), 2233–2240.

caveats: A yes given to spare feelings is one more reason a yes is never counted.
app: Every ask on the path is plain and easy to decline, and a date ends with a clear, kind word from you.

claim: A rejection lingers when it changes how a person defines themselves, most for those who believe personality cannot change.
effect: across five studies, people who saw personality as fixed tied past and imagined rejections to their self-definition and felt haunted by them for longer
population: adults recalling or imagining rejection

sources.cite: Howe & Dweck (2016). Changes in self-definition impede recovery from rejection. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 42(1), 54–71.

caveats: Recalled and imagined rejection.
app: A rep is complete whatever the answer, so a no is never a verdict on you in the record.

claim: Persisting after a no is at the heart of stalking and harassment: much unwanted pursuit grows out of courtship that did not take no for an answer.
effect: a review of 175 studies of stalking: pursuit most often arises from prior or desired relationships
population: a review of stalking research

sources.cite: Spitzberg & Cupach (2007). The state of the art of stalking: taking stock of the emerging literature. Aggression and Violent Behavior, 12(1), 64–86.

caveats: A review of harm, read as a boundary rather than a statistic.
app: One ask, and anything other than a yes is final; a second ask after a no is never offered.

claim: Unwanted attention from strangers in public is common for women and goes with feeling objectified.
effect: women reported frequent stranger harassment, which went with self-objectification and fear
population: college women in survey studies

sources.cite: Fairchild & Rudman (2008). Everyday stranger harassment and women’s objectification. Social Justice Research, 21(3), 338–357.

caveats: Surveys of students.
app: Approaching strangers in the street is excluded from the Partner path.

claim: Endorsing assertive pickup tactics tracks hostile sexism.
effect: hostile sexism predicted endorsing and using assertive courtship strategies
population: adults in survey studies

sources.cite: Hall & Canterberry (2011). Sexism and assertive courtship strategies. Sex Roles, 65(11–12), 840–853.

caveats: Correlational surveys.
app: Lines, tactics and games are excluded from the Partner path.

claim: Several changes in who lives in a child’s home go with more behaviour problems, partly because of what came before; one study found a mother’s dating after divorce had little direct effect; when to introduce a new partner has no tested answer.
effect: transitions related to behavioural outcomes, perhaps causally in part, while cognitive links were explained by prior characteristics (Fomby and Cherlin 2007); a systematic review found support mixed (Hadfield 2018); mothers’ dating transitions had little direct effect on children’s adjustment (Xiao 2022); few evidence-based guidelines exist for sharing dating with children (Kang and Nielson 2025)
population: US children and families; a systematic review; post-divorce families

sources.cite: Fomby & Cherlin (2007). Family instability and child well-being. American Sociological Review, 72(2), 181–204.

Hadfield, Amos, Ungar, Gosselin & Ganong (2018). Do changes to family structure affect child and family outcomes? A systematic review of the instability hypothesis. Journal of Family Theory & Review, 10(1), 87–110.
Xiao, Langlais & Anderson (2022). Is it OK if mommy dates? The influence of mother’s post-divorce dating transitions on children’s well-being. Journal of Child and Family Studies, 31(2), 400–413.

Kang & Nielson (2025). Helping postdivorce families enhance parent–child relationships: clinical applications for communicating postdivorce dating with children. Journal of Marital and Family Therapy, 51(1), e12764.

caveats: Mostly mothers; the timing of introductions is expert opinion.
app: General guidance for a parent in the Partner path’s text, and the considerations before introducing a partner to your child; the path never schedules an introduction.

claim: Shared religious practice at home goes with better relationship quality, modestly, and part of it is who chooses to share it.
effect: couples’ in-home devotional activities and shared beliefs were positively linked with relationship quality (Ellison 2010); reviews of religion in families find mostly small, mixed associations (Mahoney 2001, 2010)
population: US couples; reviews of family research

sources.cite: Ellison, Burdette & Wilcox (2010). The couple that prays together: race and ethnicity, religion, and relationship quality among working-age adults. Journal of Marriage and Family, 72(4), 963–975.
Mahoney (2010). Religion in families, 1999–2009: a relational spirituality framework. Journal of Marriage and Family, 72(4), 805–827.

Mahoney, Pargament, Tarakeshwar & Swank (2001). Religion in the home in the 1980s and 1990s: a meta-analytic review and conceptual analysis of links between religion, marriage, and parenting. Journal of Family Psychology, 15(4), 559–596.

caveats: Correlational; selection is likely.
app: Context for the Partner path; never a requirement of anyone.

claim: A relationship’s quality is predicted mostly by each person’s own view of the relationship, their sense of the partner’s commitment and appreciation, conflict and satisfaction, and hardly at all by the partner’s reported traits.
effect: machine learning across 43 longitudinal datasets: relationship-specific variables predicted up to 45 percent of variance at baseline and 18 percent later; one’s own reports predicted two to four times more than the partner’s
population: couples in 43 longitudinal datasets

sources.cite: Joel et al. (2020). Machine learning uncovers the most robust self-report predictors of relationship quality across 43 longitudinal couples studies. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 117(32), 19061–19071.

caveats: Self-report; prediction, not cause.
app: Choosing well is attending to how the relationship works and to your own side, never a quiz of traits.

claim: In existing relationships, actual similarity between partners barely predicts satisfaction; perceived similarity does.
effect: couple similarity in personality explained under half a percent of satisfaction in three national samples (Dyrenforth 2010); a meta-analysis of 313 studies found actual similarity mattered in brief encounters and not in existing relationships, where perceived similarity still predicted attraction (Montoya 2008)
population: national couple samples; a meta-analysis of 460 effects

sources.cite: Dyrenforth, Kashy, Donnellan & Lucas (2010). Predicting relationship and life satisfaction from personality in nationally representative samples from three countries: the relative importance of actor, partner, and similarity effects. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 99(4), 690–702.
Montoya, Horton & Kirchner (2008). Is actual similarity necessary for attraction? A meta-analysis of actual and perceived similarity. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 25(6), 889–922.

caveats: Personality similarity; shared values were measured less.
app: No compatibility score and no opposites-attract either.

claim: People weigh a partner’s dealbreakers more heavily than the qualities they hope for, so knowing your own few non-negotiables in advance is useful.
effect: across studies, dealbreakers counted more negatively than dealmakers counted positively, more so for women and for people in committed relationships
population: adults in several survey studies

sources.cite: Jonason, Garcia, Webster, Li & Fisher (2015). Relationship dealbreakers: traits people avoid in potential mates. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 41(12), 1697–1711.

caveats: Stated, not observed, choices.
app: The values note in three parts, from the start of the Partner path: a few true non-negotiables, preferences held loosely, and the partner you want to be.

claim: A person’s own negative affectivity and insecure attachment weigh on relationship quality, and both can change with effort.
effect: a review of longitudinal marriage research (Karney and Bradbury 1995); anxious and avoidant attachment both harmed relationship quality in a meta-analysis (Li and Chan 2012); interventions changed personality traits, d ≈ .37 over about 24 weeks (Roberts 2017); wanting to become less anxious or avoidant predicted that change (Hudson 2020)
population: married couples; meta-analyses; adults in longitudinal studies

sources.cite: Karney & Bradbury (1995). The longitudinal course of marital quality and stability: a review of theory, methods, and research. Psychological Bulletin, 118(1), 3–34.
Li & Chan (2012). How anxious and avoidant attachment affect romantic relationship quality differently: a meta-analytic review. European Journal of Social Psychology, 42(4), 406–419.
Roberts et al. (2017). A systematic review of personality trait change through intervention. Psychological Bulletin, 143(2), 117–141.

Hudson, Chopik & Briley (2020). Volitional change in adult attachment: can people who want to become less anxious and avoidant move closer towards realizing those goals? European Journal of Personality, 34(1), 93–114.

caveats: Change is modest and slow; the trait studies are mostly clinical interventions.
app: The Partner path works on your own side, the part you can change, and never labels a partner’s attachment.

claim: People who decide their relationship steps thoughtfully report more dedication and satisfaction than those who slide into them, and couples who moved in together before engagement reported somewhat poorer marriages.
effect: thoughtful decision-making went with more dedication and satisfaction across dating, cohabiting and married people, n = 252 (Owen 2013); cohabiting before engagement went with lower satisfaction and dedication, small differences (Rhoades 2009); the sliding argument (Stanley 2006)
population: US adults in surveys

sources.cite: Stanley, Rhoades & Markman (2006). Sliding versus deciding: inertia and the premarital cohabitation effect. Family Relations, 55(4), 499–509.
Rhoades, Stanley & Markman (2009). The pre-engagement cohabitation effect: a replication and extension of previous findings. Journal of Family Psychology, 23(1), 107–111.
Owen, Rhoades & Stanley (2013). Sliding versus deciding in relationships: associations with relationship quality, commitment, and infidelity. Journal of Couple & Relationship Therapy, 12(2), 135–149.

caveats: The general cohabitation effect is contested; selection is part of it.
app: The decide-don’t-slide notes, from the Dating stage on, each written with your own record in front of you.

claim: Relationship education improves couples’ communication, modestly; effects on quality are smaller and uncertain once unpublished studies count, and moderate courses of nine to twenty hours beat short ones.
effect: experimental studies: relationship quality d = .30 to .36, communication d = .43 to .45 (Hawkins 2008); premarital programmes did not improve quality with unpublished studies included but improved communication (Fawcett 2010); 9–20 contact hours beat 1–8 (Hawkins 2012); self-directed programmes alone: quality d = .03, not significant (McAllister 2012)
population: couples in evaluation studies and meta-analyses

sources.cite: Hawkins, Blanchard, Baldwin & Fawcett (2008). Does marriage and relationship education work? A meta-analytic study. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 76(5), 723–734.
Fawcett, Hawkins, Blanchard & Carroll (2010). Do premarital education programs really work? A meta-analytic study. Family Relations, 59(3), 232–239.

Hawkins, Stanley, Blanchard & Albright (2012). Exploring programmatic moderators of the effectiveness of marriage and relationship education programs: a meta-analytic study. Behavior Therapy, 43(1), 77–87.
McAllister, Duncan & Hawkins (2012). Examining the early evidence for self-directed marriage and relationship education: a meta-analytic study. Family Relations, 61(5), 742–755.

caveats: Modest effects; reading alone did little.
app: Education before a commitment at the Deciding stage: a course together, not a book on your own.

claim: The number and frequency of early warning signs in a relationship, such as reacting badly to a no or resenting questions, predicted abuse six months later.
effect: warning signs and protective factors predicted overall, physical, psychological and sexual abuse cross-sectionally and prospectively over six months
population: university and online samples of adults in relationships

sources.cite: Charlot et al. (2023). The predictive validity of intimate partner violence warning signs. Social Psychological and Personality Science.

caveats: Two studies; a sign is a reason to look closer, not a verdict on a person.
app: The monthly private check asks about your own safety and conduct; its fixed help is the app’s, never a model’s.

claim: How couples talk predicts how they fare, modestly: negative communication goes with lower later quality and with breaking up, and hostility weighs most.
effect: a meta-analysis of 64 dyadic studies: positive r ≈ .15 and negative r ≈ −.17 with later quality; negative communication d = −0.41 with dissolution (Kanter 2022); hostility robustly tied to lower satisfaction (Woodin 2011); demand-withdraw r ≈ .38 to .39 with poorer outcomes (Schrodt 2014)
population: couples in dyadic studies and meta-analyses

sources.cite: Kanter et al. (2022). Does couple communication predict later relationship quality and dissolution? A meta-analysis. Journal of Marriage and Family, 84(2), 533–551.
Woodin (2011). A two-dimensional approach to relationship conflict: meta-analytic findings. Journal of Family Psychology, 25(3), 325–335.

Schrodt, Witt & Shimkowski (2014). A meta-analytical review of the demand/withdraw pattern of interaction and its associations with individual, relational, and communicative outcomes. Communication Monographs, 81(1), 28–58.

caveats: Associations of modest size; they do not sort couples into futures.
app: The reappraisal rep and the good-news rep work on the talk itself; nothing tallies conflicts.

claim: How a partner responds to good news matters: active, enthusiastic responses go with closer, more satisfying relationships, more so than responses to bad news.
effect: sharing good news raised daily positive feeling, and enthusiastic partner responses went with more intimacy and satisfaction (Gable 2004); two months on, responses to good news predicted well-being and break-up better than responses to bad news (Gable 2006)
population: couples in diary and observational studies

sources.cite: Gable, Reis, Impett & Asher (2004). What do you do when things go right? The intrapersonal and interpersonal benefits of sharing positive events. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 87(2), 228–245.
Gable, Gonzaga & Strachman (2006). Will you be there for me when things go right? Supportive responses to positive event disclosures. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 91(5), 904–917.

caveats: Correlational and observational.
app: The respond-to-good-news rep at the Building stage.

claim: Everyday gratitude between partners predicts more connection and satisfaction the next day for both, and expressing it in a lab session helped when the partner responded well.
effect: in daily diaries, gratitude from thoughtful benefits predicted next-day connection and satisfaction for recipient and benefactor (Algoe 2010); a randomised gratitude expression had modest effects overall (Algoe and Zhaoyang 2016)
population: cohabiting couples in diary and experimental studies

sources.cite: Algoe, Gable & Maisel (2010). It’s the little things: everyday gratitude as a booster shot for romantic relationships. Personal Relationships, 17(2), 217–233.

Algoe & Zhaoyang (2016). Positive psychology in context: effects of expressing gratitude in ongoing relationships depend on perceptions of enactor responsiveness. The Journal of Positive Psychology, 11(4), 399–415.

caveats: Modest effects in the experiment.
app: Thanking them for one specific thing, from the Dating stage on.

claim: Doing novel, lively things together raises couples’ experienced relationship quality.
effect: three experiments: a seven-minute novel task raised relationship quality more than a mundane one (Aron 2000); a four-week online programme of exciting activities raised excitement, positive affect and satisfaction, held at four months (Coulter and Malouff 2013)
population: couples in experiments and a randomised trial

sources.cite: Aron, Norman, Aron, McKenna & Heyman (2000). Couples’ shared participation in novel and arousing activities and experienced relationship quality. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 273–284.

Coulter & Malouff (2013). Effects of an intervention designed to enhance romantic relationship excitement: a randomized-control trial. Couple and Family Psychology: Research and Practice, 2(1), 34–44.

caveats: Short tasks and a self-selected online sample.
app: The something-new-together rep at the Building stage.

claim: A brief exercise in seeing a disagreement as a neutral third party would, done three times across a year, stopped the usual decline in marital quality.
effect: 120 couples over two years: marital quality declined in year one for all and kept declining in controls, but not among couples given the 21-minute reappraisal intervention, through less conflict-related distress
population: married couples in a two-year randomised study

sources.cite: Finkel, Slotter, Luchies, Walton & Gross (2013). A brief intervention to promote conflict reappraisal preserves marital quality over time. Psychological Science, 24(8), 1595–1601.

caveats: One trial, in 120 married couples: never replicated and never tested in dating couples. Reading a partner kindly helped healthy marriages and harmed troubled ones, so it is not for something serious or recurring.
app: The reappraise-a-disagreement rep, from the Dating stage on, labelled as one trial in married couples and guarded against explaining away what keeps happening.

claim: Couples who talk about sex, and talk about it well, report more relationship and sexual satisfaction.
effect: a meta-analysis of 93 studies, 38,499 people: r = .37 with relationship satisfaction and .43 with sexual satisfaction; the quality of the communication mattered more than its frequency
population: adults in current relationships

sources.cite: Mallory (2022). Dimensions of couples’ sexual communication, relationship satisfaction, and sexual satisfaction: a meta-analysis. Journal of Family Psychology, 36(3), 358–371.

caveats: Correlational.
app: The talk-openly rep at the Keeping stage.

claim: Forgiveness and sacrifice help a relationship in context, not unconditionally: forgiving a partner who is often negative went with worse outcomes over time, and sacrifices made reluctantly cost the one who made them.
effect: forgiveness interacted with the partner’s negative behaviour to predict marital outcomes longitudinally (McNulty 2008); a meta-analysis of 82 datasets: willingness to sacrifice went with better well-being, behavioural sacrifice with slightly lower personal well-being, r = −.07 (Righetti 2020)
population: newlyweds; couples across 82 datasets

sources.cite: McNulty (2008). Forgiveness in marriage: putting the benefits into context. Journal of Family Psychology, 22(1), 171–175.
Righetti et al. (2020). The link between sacrifice and relational and personal well-being: a meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 146(10), 900–921.

caveats: Context matters in both directions.
app: No rep asks for unconditional forgiveness or sacrifice.

claim: On days of higher outside stress, partners behave more negatively toward each other and judge the relationship less kindly.
effect: external stress went with the trajectory of marital quality (Neff and Karney 2004); under greater stress, daily satisfaction tracked daily events more strongly (Neff and Karney 2009); on higher-stress days spouses reported more negative behaviour and fewer positive appraisals (Buck and Neff 2012)
population: newlywed couples in diary studies

sources.cite: Neff & Karney (2004). How does context affect intimate relationships? Linking external stress and cognitive processes within marriage. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 30(2), 134–148.
Neff & Karney (2009). Stress and reactivity to daily relationship experiences: how stress hinders adaptive processes in marriage. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 97(3), 435–450.
Buck & Neff (2012). Stress spillover in early marriage: the role of self-regulatory depletion. Journal of Family Psychology, 26(5), 698–708.

caveats: Newlyweds; stress is self-reported.
app: On a day the record reads high stress or overwhelm, only light reps are offered and no evaluative prompt is shown.

claim: Keeping a detailed diary about relationship conflict can itself shift how people rate their relationship, even when their behaviour does not change.
effect: fifteen days of conflict diaries left observed behaviour unchanged, while husbands’ self-reports of marital quality fell over the recording period
population: married couples, a diary group and a non-randomised control

sources.cite: Merrilees, Goeke-Morey & Cummings (2008). Do event-contingent diaries about marital conflict change marital interactions? Behaviour Research and Therapy, 46(2), 253–262.

caveats: Non-randomised control; small reactivity signals.
app: The monthly reflection asks about one moment at a time and your own part in it, once a month, and never a daily verdict.

claim: Partners whose goals fit report more satisfaction, and among people who were dating, seeing their relationship goals as shared went with a better relationship.
effect: a meta-analysis of 49 samples: goal congruence r = .43 with satisfaction, goal support .28, goal conflict −.29 (Toma 2022); in 245 dating people and 78 diary couples, perceived mutuality of relationship goals predicted quality through a sense of progress (Avivi 2009); newly dating partners who gave up clashing goals grew more committed, but women were less satisfied when the partner was the one giving ground (Gere and Impett 2017)
population: couples of all kinds; dating samples in two studies

sources.cite: Toma et al. (2022). The role of goal interdependence in couples’ relationship satisfaction: A meta-analysis. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 40(6), 1740–1769.
Avivi et al. (2009). Linking Relationship Quality to Perceived Mutuality of Relationship Goals and Perceived Goal Progress. Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 28(2), 137–164.
Gere and Impett (2017). Shifting priorities. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 35(6), 793–810.

caveats: Correlational; goals range from daily plans to life goals; no study tests whether talking about them changes what follows.
app: The direction talks at the Dating stage: learning where your lives point, never a test either of you passes.

claim: Avoiding talk about where a relationship stands comes with more uncertainty, and weeks later with less dedication and satisfaction.
effect: 244 emerging adults: avoiding relationship talk followed uncertainty seven weeks earlier and predicted lower dedication and satisfaction seven weeks later (Clifford 2017); in courting couples, avoiding the talk raised the next week’s uncertainty (Knobloch and Theiss 2011); the state of the relationship was the most common taboo topic (Baxter and Wilmot 1985)
population: dating couples and emerging adults

sources.cite: Clifford et al. (2017). Testing the impact of sliding versus deciding in cyclical and noncyclical relationships. Personal Relationships, 24(1), 223–238.
Knobloch and Theiss (2011). Relational Uncertainty and Relationship Talk within Courtship: A Longitudinal Actor–Partner Interdependence Model. Communication Monographs, 78(1), 3–26.
Baxter and Wilmot (1985). Taboo Topics in Close Relationships. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 2(3), 253–269.

caveats: Self-report over weeks; sliding was measured as avoiding the talk.
app: Why the path offers the direction talks during Dating instead of leaving them to chance.

claim: Closeness grows through disclosure that deepens step by step and goes both ways; in one study a very personal disclosure early in a first conversation was liked less than the same one made later.
effect: turn-taking reciprocal disclosure brought more liking and closeness than one-sided disclosure (Sprecher and Treger 2015); an intimate disclosure early in a ten-minute conversation was liked less than one made late (Wortman 1976); gradually escalating questions built closeness between strangers (Aron 1997)
population: strangers and new acquaintances in laboratory conversations

sources.cite: Sprecher and Treger (2015). The benefits of turn‐taking reciprocal self‐disclosure in get‐acquainted interactions. Personal Relationships, 22(3), 460–475.
Wortman et al. (1976). Self-disclosure: An attributional perspective. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 33(2), 184–191.
Aron et al. (1997). The Experimental Generation of Interpersonal Closeness: A Procedure and Some Preliminary Findings. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 23(4), 363–377.

caveats: Laboratory conversations between strangers; no study says when a couple should raise a given topic.
app: The lighter direction talks come first, and the weightier ones join the app’s picks once they are done.

claim: When partners disagree about having a child, fewer children follow, and births one partner did not intend go with more separation and divorce.
effect: couple-level panels: disagreement pushed both partners toward no child (Thomson 1997); half the couples who disagreed about a first child had one, and a disagreement about another child usually meant none (Testa and Bolano 2021); first births the father did not intend raised the risk of divorce (Stykes and Guzzo 2020)
population: married and cohabiting couples in the United States and Australia

sources.cite: Testa and Bolano (2021). When partners’ disagreement prevents childbearing: A couple-level analysis in Australia. Demographic Research, 44, 811–838.
Thomson (1997). Couple childbearing desires, intentions, and births. Demography, 34(3), 343–354.
Stykes and Guzzo (2020). Unintended Childbearing and Marital Instability: An Emphasis on Couples’ Intentions. Journal of Divorce & Remarriage, 61(7), 504–524.

caveats: The outcome is mostly births, not the relationship; no study follows dating couples’ agreement about children to a later breakup.
app: The children-and-family talk at the Dating stage, and parenting roles before moving in.

claim: An earlier first talk about money went with better money communication and relationship quality, and in married and cohabiting couples money disagreements predicted divorce and breakup more than other disagreements.
effect: 1,950 US emerging adults: an earlier first talk about money went with better money communication and, through it, higher relationship quality, and with slightly more money conflict (Saxey 2022); 4,574 married couples: money disagreements predicted divorce more than other disagreements, through how conflicts were handled (Dew, Britt and Huston 2012); cohabiting partners’ money disagreements predicted breakup (Dew 2011)
population: emerging adults in relationships; married and cohabiting couples

sources.cite: Saxey et al. (2022). The Sooner, the Better? Couples' First Financial Discussion, Relationship Quality, and Financial Conflict in Emerging Adulthood. Journal of Financial Therapy, 13(1).
Dew et al. (2012). Examining the Relationship Between Financial Issues and Divorce. Family Relations, 61(4), 615–628.
Dew (2011). Financial Issues and Relationship Outcomes Among Cohabiting Individuals. Family Relations, 60(2), 178–190.

caveats: The talk-timing study is one survey at one time; the rest are married or cohabiting couples.
app: The work, money and home talk at Dating, and money together before moving in.

claim: Among dating and cohabiting adults, shared beliefs and practice go with more satisfaction; in marriages, gaps in practice go with more conflict and divorce, and how faith is talked about matters.
effect: 468 unmarried adults: shared beliefs, joint attendance and seeing the relationship as sacred went with higher satisfaction (Henderson, Ellison and Glenn 2017); 4,587 married couples: divorce risk was lowest when both attended and higher when attendance differed (Call and Heaton 1997); sharing spiritual views predicted less conflict, and using faith to claim the upper hand predicted stalemate (Mahoney, Pargament and DeMaris 2021)
population: unmarried adults; married couples

sources.cite: Henderson et al. (2017). Religion and Relationship Quality Among Cohabiting and Dating Couples. Journal of Family Issues, 39(7), 1904–1932.
Call and Heaton (1997). Religious Influence on Marital Stability. Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion, 36(3), 382.
Mahoney et al. (2021). Spiritual intimacy, spiritual one-upmanship, and marital conflict across the transition to parenthood. Journal of Family Psychology, 35(4), 552–558.

caveats: Correlational and shaped by who chooses whom; whether denomination or practice matters more is contested.
app: The faith talks, shown only while the faith family is shown; never a requirement of anyone.

claim: Feeling appreciated by a partner goes with appreciating them in turn, being more responsive and committed, and staying together; your own gratitude predicts rising commitment whatever your partner’s.
effect: a multimethod series: people who felt appreciated appreciated their partners more, were more responsive and committed, and more likely to remain together over time (Gordon 2012); seeing a partner invest brought gratitude and then commitment (Joel 2013); in six longitudinal couple datasets (562 couples), a person’s own gratitude predicted rising commitment regardless of the partner’s (Park 2023)
population: romantic couples, dating and married

sources.cite: Gordon et al. (2012). To have and to hold: Gratitude promotes relationship maintenance in intimate bonds. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 103(2), 257–274.
Joel et al. (2013). The Things You Do for Me. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 39(10), 1333–1345.
Park et al. (2023). Differing Levels of Gratitude Between Romantic Partners: Concurrent and Longitudinal Links With Satisfaction and Commitment in Six Dyadic Datasets. Personality Science, 4(1).

caveats: Mostly correlational; the chain from appreciation to staying together is not an experiment.
app: Thanking them for one specific thing, from the Dating stage on.

claim: Whether a dating relationship lasts is predicted by how it works, commitment, love and closeness, far more than by personality, and swings in satisfaction or in how committed the partner seems predict breakup beyond their average.
effect: a meta-analysis of 137 studies (37,761 people): commitment, love, inclusion of the other in the self and dependence predicted breakup most, personality little (Le 2010); fluctuation in satisfaction predicted breakup beyond its level (Arriaga 2001); fluctuation in perceived partner commitment did too (Arriaga 2006)
population: people in dating relationships

sources.cite: Le et al. (2010). Predicting nonmarital romantic relationship dissolution: A meta-analytic synthesis. Personal Relationships, 17(3), 377–390.
Arriaga (2001). The ups and downs of dating: Fluctuations in satisfaction in newly formed romantic relationships. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 80(5), 754–765.

Arriaga et al. (2006). Relationship perceptions and persistence: Do fluctuations in perceived partner commitment undermine dating relationships?. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 91(6), 1045–1065.

caveats: Prediction, not cause; one moment’s rating says little on its own, and the app computes nothing from yours.
app: The monthly reflection keeps your own record of how it works, month by month, in words.

claim: People remember their relationship’s past to fit how they feel now, and their own ratings at the time predicted its future better than their forecasts did.
effect: dating partners’ recall of earlier ratings drifted toward their current impressions (McFarland and Ross 1987); students’ forecasts about their dating relationships were overly optimistic, while their own quality ratings predicted stability a year on best (MacDonald and Ross 1999); newlyweds recalled a decline and a recent improvement where their ratings showed a steady decline (Karney and Frye 2002)
population: dating partners and newlyweds

sources.cite: McFarland and Ross (1987). The Relation between Current Impressions and Memories of Self and Dating Partners. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 13(2), 228–238.

MacDonald and Ross (1999). Assessing the Accuracy of Predictions about Dating Relationships: How and Why Do Lovers’ Predictions Differ from those Made by Observers?. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 25(11), 1417–1429.

Karney and Frye (2002). "But we've been getting better lately": Comparing prospective and retrospective views of relationship development. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 82(2), 222–238.

caveats: No study compares deciding from a written record with deciding from memory.
app: Before each decide-don’t-slide note, your own record is shown read-only, as you wrote it.

claim: A little reflection on a relationship helped in two trials, writing about a dating relationship and one session discussing films about couples, while a daily prompt did nothing.
effect: 86 dating couples: the partner who wrote about the relationship for three days made staying together at three months likelier (Slatcher and Pennebaker 2006); 174 engaged or newly married couples: one guided session of discussing relationship films matched two skills courses on breakup at three years among completers (Rogge 2013); 461 students: a daily text for 28 days brought no gains (Hatch 2019)
population: dating, engaged and newly married couples; college students

sources.cite: Slatcher and Pennebaker (2006). How Do I Love Thee? Let Me Count the Words. Psychological Science, 17(8), 660–664.

Rogge et al. (2013). Is skills training necessary for the primary prevention of marital distress and dissolution? A 3-year experimental study of three interventions. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 81(6), 949–961.
Hatch et al. (2019). Texts 4 Romantic Relationships – A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Couple & Relationship Therapy, 19(2), 115–135.

caveats: Single trials, not replicated; one compared completers; no trial varies how often to reflect.
app: The monthly reflection: once a month, optional, a few lines, never a score.

claim: People lean toward letting relationships go on, staying partly for the partner’s sake and settling more when they fear being single, while doubts before marrying and commitment that runs unequal both predict trouble.
effect: 1,348 people and a preregistered replication: those who believed their partner depended on them were less likely to start a breakup (Joel 2018); fear of being single predicted settling for less (Spielmann 2013); women’s premarital doubts predicted divorce four years on (Lavner, Karney and Bradbury 2012); in 315 unmarried couples, lopsided commitment went with more breakups (Stanley 2016)
population: single, dating and newly married people

sources.cite: Joel et al. (2018). How interdependent are stay/leave decisions? On staying in the relationship for the sake of the romantic partner. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 115(5), 805–824.
Spielmann et al. (2013). Settling for less out of fear of being single. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 105(6), 1049–1073.
Lavner et al. (2012). Do cold feet warn of trouble ahead? Premarital uncertainty and four-year marital outcomes. Journal of Family Psychology, 26(6), 1012–1017.
Stanley et al. (2016). Asymmetrically committed relationships. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 34(8), 1241–1259.

caveats: Mostly correlational; doubts were recalled after the wedding; one of the settling studies carries a 2018 correction to its scale.
app: The decide-don’t-slide notes, written with your own record in front of you.

claim: Little is known about when to introduce a partner to a child; children who had grown close to a parent’s dating partner struggled more when it ended, and a close bond between parent and child softened a parent’s dating.
effect: 270 divorced mothers and 170 children: breakups had no effect overall, but children close to the mother’s partner showed more anxiety and withdrawal when it ended (Langlais 2018); stepfathers’ friendship-building went with better step-relationships and marriages (Ganong 2019); a review of 37 studies tied close parent–child bonds and support for the step-relationship to better child outcomes (Sanner 2022)
population: divorced mothers and their children; stepfamilies

sources.cite: Langlais et al. (2018). The Impact of Mothers’ Post-Divorce Dating Breakups on Children’s Problem Behaviors. Journal of Child and Family Studies, 27(8), 2643–2655.

Ganong et al. (2019). Stepfathers’ affinity-seeking with stepchildren, stepfather-stepchild relationship quality, marital quality, and stepfamily cohesion among stepfathers and mothers. Journal of Family Psychology, 33(5), 521–531.
Sanner et al. (2022). Effective parenting in stepfamilies: Empirical evidence of what works. Family Relations, 71(3), 884–899.

caveats: Almost all from mothers after divorce, nothing on fathers raising a child; when to introduce is expert opinion.
app: Introducing them to your child: a deliberate decision point, never scheduled or recommended by the app.

claim: Reading a partner’s behaviour kindly helped healthy marriages and was followed by steeper declines in troubled ones.
effect: 251 newlywed couples: kind interpretations of a partner’s behaviour predicted better outcomes where problems were mild, and steeper declines where they were frequent or severe
population: newlywed couples

sources.cite: McNulty et al. (2008). Benevolent cognitions as a strategy of relationship maintenance: "Don't sweat the small stuff"....But it is not all small stuff. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 94(4), 631–646.

caveats: One sample of newlyweds.
app: The reappraisal rep’s guard: for ordinary disagreements, never for explaining away something serious or recurring.

claim: Couples assigned to pool their money kept their relationship quality over two years while other couples’ declined, and pooling goes with satisfaction across many studies.
effect: a randomised trial of engaged and newly married couples: those assigned a joint account kept their relationship quality over two years (Olson 2023); six studies (N = 38,534): pooling finances went with satisfaction (Gladstone 2022)
population: engaged and newly married couples; adults in relationships

sources.cite: Olson et al. (2023). Common Cents: Bank Account Structure and Couples’ Relationship Dynamics. Journal of Consumer Research, 50(4), 704–721.
Gladstone et al. (2022). Pooling finances and relationship satisfaction. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 123(6), 1293–1314.

caveats: One trial; the app never prescribes how a couple organises money.
app: Evidence beside talking money through before moving in.

claim: Seeing the split of housework as unfair lowers both partners’ happiness, feeling appreciated removes much of that, and unmet expectations about sharing childcare lower satisfaction after a birth.
effect: couples where both worked: perceived unfairness lowered happiness for both and raised divorce odds for wives (Frisco and Williams 2003); 2,193 cohabiting people: the harm of an unequal division disappeared when people felt appreciated (Gordon 2022); violated expectations about childcare predicted new parents’ satisfaction better than the actual division did (Biehle and Mickelson 2012)
population: married, cohabiting and new-parent couples

sources.cite: Frisco and Williams (2003). Perceived Housework Equity, Marital Happiness, and Divorce in Dual-Earner Households. Journal of Family Issues, 24(1), 51–73.
Gordon et al. (2022). Feeling Appreciated Buffers Against the Negative Effects of Unequal Division of Household Labor on Relationship Satisfaction. Psychological Science, 33(8), 1313–1327.
Biehle and Mickelson (2012). First-time parents' expectations about the division of childcare and play. Journal of Family Psychology, 26(1), 36–45.

caveats: Married and cohabiting couples; correlational.
app: Talking through a normal week living together, before moving in.

claim: Claims that divorce can be predicted with high accuracy from a few observed behaviours are disputed: they collapse without cross-validation, and a major model failed to replicate.
effect: prediction equations without cross-validation and base rates overstate accuracy (Heyman and Slep 2001); Gottman and colleagues’ affective process models failed to replicate (Kim 2007)
population: couples in prediction studies

sources.cite: Heyman & Slep (2001). The hazards of predicting divorce without crossvalidation. Journal of Marriage and Family, 63(2), 473–479.
Kim, Capaldi & Crosby (2007). Generalizability of Gottman and colleagues’ affective process models of couples’ relationship outcomes. Journal of Marriage and Family, 69(1), 55–72.

caveats: Kept as disputed so the brain never cites divorce prediction or its tallies.
app: Excluded from the Partner path.

claim: The popular claims about love languages are disputed: the evidence does not support that each person has one preferred language, that there are five, or that matching them makes couples happier.
effect: a review found little empirical support for the three central assumptions
population: a review of the empirical literature

sources.cite: Impett, Park & Muise (2024). Popular psychology through a scientific lens: evaluating love languages from a relationship science perspective. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 33(2), 87–92.

caveats: Kept as disputed so the brain never cites love languages.
app: Excluded from the Partner path.

claim: The claim that dating sites’ matching algorithms find compatible partners is disputed: no compelling evidence supports it, and traits measured in advance cannot predict which pairs will click.
effect: a review found no compelling evidence for matching algorithms (Finkel 2012); 100+ pre-date measures predicted none of the desire unique to a pair (Joel 2017)
population: a review; speed daters

sources.cite: Finkel, Eastwick, Karney, Reis & Sprecher (2012). Online dating: a critical analysis from the perspective of psychological science. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 13(1), 3–66.
Joel, Eastwick & Finkel (2017). Is romantic desire predictable? Machine learning applied to initial romantic attraction. Psychological Science, 28(10), 1478–1489.

caveats: Kept as disputed so the brain never cites a compatibility match.
app: Excluded from the Partner path.
